records.content:
Notice the pattern in every example:

Standardize: Convert Y-values to Z-values using z = (y - \mu)/\sigma.

Look up: Find the probability using the Z-table or R’s pnorm().

Unstandardize (if needed): Convert Z-values back to Y-values using y = \mu + z\sigma.

This three-step pattern works for every Normal probability problem. The key R functions:

Function

What It Computes

pnorm(y, mu, sigma)

P(Y \leq y) — CDF

pnorm(y, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)

P(Y > y) — right tail

qnorm(p, mu, sigma)

\phi_p — the pth quantile

dnorm(y, mu, sigma)

f(y) — the density (not a probability!)

rnorm(n, mu, sigma)

Generate n random Normal values# Simulate: verify the 68-95-99.7 rule
set.seed(2026)
Y <- rnorm(1000000, mean = 50, sd = 10)
mean(abs(Y - 50) < 10)   # ≈ 0.6827 (within 1 SD)
mean(abs(Y - 50) < 20)   # ≈ 0.9545 (within 2 SDs)
mean(abs(Y - 50) < 30)   # ≈ 0.9973 (within 3 SDs)

⚠️ Common Mistakes — The Normal Distribution

Writing N(\mu, \sigma) instead of N(\mu, \sigma^2). The second parameter of N(\mu, \sigma^2) is the variance, not the standard deviation. If Y \sim N(100, 25), then \sigma^2 = 25 and \sigma = 5. Some textbooks use the convention N(\mu, \sigma) — this book uses N(\mu, \sigma^2), and so does the reference textbook.

Forgetting to standardize. You cannot look up P(Y > 78) directly in the Z-table if Y \sim N(72, 64). You must first compute z = (78 - 72)/8 = 0.75 and then look up P(Z > 0.75).

Using the wrong tail. If the table gives A(z) = P(Z > z), then P(Z < z) = 1 - A(z), and P(Z < -z) = A(z) by symmetry. Draw a picture every time until the pattern becomes automatic.

Confusing f(y) with P(Y = y). The Normal density f(y) can be computed with dnorm(), but this is the height of the bell curve, not a probability. For continuous distributions, P(Y = y) = 0 always. Use pnorm() for probabilities.

Thinking the Normal distribution is bounded. The Normal distribution extends from -\infty to +\infty. A N(500, 25) model technically assigns positive probability to negative values — but P(Y < 0) = P(Z < -100) \approx 0, which is effectively zero. In practice, this is fine.

5.5.1. Let Z \sim N(0, 1). Find:

(a) P(Z > 1.96)
(b) P(-1.5 < Z < 0.5)
(c) P(|Z| > 2.33)
(d) The value c such that P(-c < Z < c) = 0.90

5.5.2. The diastolic blood pressure of adult males is Normally distributed with mean 82 mmHg and standard deviation 10 mmHg.

(a) What proportion of men have blood pressure above 100 mmHg?
(b) A man is classified as having “high blood pressure” if his reading exceeds 90 mmHg. What proportion of men fall in this category?
(c) A health study recruits men with blood pressure between 70 and 90 mmHg. What proportion of the male population is eligible?
(d) What blood pressure value marks the 95th percentile?

5.5.3. A machine fills cereal boxes. The weight of cereal per box is N(368, 16) grams. The label says 360 grams.

(a) What proportion of boxes are underweight (less than 360 g)?
(b) The company wants at most 2% of boxes to be underweight. If \mu cannot be changed, what is the maximum allowable \sigma?
(c) Alternatively, if \sigma = 4 is fixed, what mean \mu would ensure at most 2% underweight?

5.5.4. Two lightbulbs are installed in a fixture. Bulb A has a lifetime that is N(900, 10000) hours and Bulb B has a lifetime that is N(1100, 22500) hours. The lifetimes are independent.

(a) Find the probability that Bulb A lasts more than 1000 hours.
(b) Let D = B - A be the difference in lifetimes. What is the distribution of D? (Hint: A linear combination of independent Normals is Normal. What are E(D) and V(D)?)
(c) Find the probability that Bulb B outlasts Bulb A by more than 300 hours.

5.5.5. (Proof) Show that if Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), then P(Y \leq \mu) = 0.5. (Hint: Use the substitution u = 2\mu - y to show that \int_{-\infty}^{\mu} f(y) \, dy = \int_{\mu}^{\infty} f(y) \, dy.)

🔬 What Did We Learn?

The Normal distribution N(\mu, \sigma^2) is the bell-shaped curve defined by two parameters: the mean \mu (the center) and the variance \sigma^2 (the spread). Its density is symmetric about \mu, and 68/95/99.7% of the probability lies within 1/2/3 standard deviations of the mean.

The key technique is standardization: convert any Normal variable Y to the standard Normal Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma, look up the probability, and convert back if needed. The Z-value tells you “how many standard deviations from the mean.”

The real-life interpretation: When a doctor says your cholesterol is “1.5 standard deviations above average,” that’s a Z-value. When a student asks “is a score of 82 good on this test?”, the answer depends on \mu and \sigma — a score of 82 on a N(75, 25) exam (z = 1.4, top 8%) is very different from 82 on a N(85, 9) exam (z = -1.0, bottom 16%). The Z-score is the universal yardstick for comparing values across different Normal distributions.

The Normal distribution also has a deep connection to other distributions we’ll study. The Chi-Square distribution (Section 5.6) arises from squaring standard Normals. The t-distribution and F-distribution (which you’ll meet in mathematical statistics) are built from ratios involving Normal and Chi-Square variables. The Normal is not just one distribution — it’s the foundation of an entire family.

Looking ahead: The next section introduces the Gamma distribution family — a versatile family of right-skewed distributions that includes the Exponential (for modeling wait times) and the Chi-Square (for statistical inference) as special cases.

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

The Normal distribution is symmetric — it works beautifully when data clusters around a central value with equal spread on both sides. But many real-world quantities are right-skewed: they have a natural lower bound (often zero), a peak near the left, and a long tail stretching to the right. Wait times, lifetimes of equipment, insurance claims, rainfall amounts — all share this shape.

The Gamma distribution is a flexible family designed for exactly these situations. It has two parameters — shape (\alpha) and scale (\beta) — that let it take on a wide range of right-skewed shapes, from sharply peaked to nearly flat.

What makes the Gamma family powerful is that it contains two famous distributions as special cases:

The Exponential distribution (\alpha = 1): models the waiting time until the next event in a Poisson process. It has the remarkable memoryless property — the probability of waiting t more minutes is the same whether you’ve been waiting 5 minutes or 5 hours.

The Chi-Square distribution (\alpha = \nu/2, \beta = 2): arises from sums of squared standard Normals. It is the foundation of hypothesis testing in mathematical statistics.

By learning the Gamma distribution first, you get all three distributions at once.

Real-life motivation: A nuclear reactor contains components whose lifetimes follow Gamma distributions. A technician needs to know: what’s the probability a component fails within the first 1,000 hours? What’s the expected replacement cost per year? The Gamma distribution answers both. Meanwhile, the call center down the road uses the Exponential distribution to model the time between incoming calls — and the quality engineer upstairs uses the Chi-Square distribution to test whether the production line meets specifications. All three are the same family.

records.content:
Before defining the Gamma distribution, we need a mathematical tool: the Gamma function.

Definition 5.10: The Gamma Function

For \alpha > 0, the Gamma function is defined by:\Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^{\infty} t^{\alpha - 1} e^{-t} \, dt

The Gamma function is an extension of the factorial to all positive real numbers (not just integers). Its key properties:

Theorem 5.10: Properties of the Gamma Function

Recursion: \Gamma(\alpha) = (\alpha - 1) \cdot \Gamma(\alpha - 1) for \alpha > 1

Factorial connection: \Gamma(n) = (n - 1)! for any positive integer n

Special value: \Gamma(1) = 1

Half-integer value: \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}

Proof of Property 1 (Recursion).

Strategy: We’ll use integration by parts on \Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^{\infty} t^{\alpha-1} e^{-t} \, dt.

📐 Calculus Flashback: Integration by Parts\int u \, dv = uv \Big|_{\text{bounds}} - \int v \, du

Choose u = the part that gets simpler when differentiated. Choose dv = the rest (which you must be able to integrate).

Set u = t^{\alpha-1} and dv = e^{-t} \, dt. Then:du = (\alpha - 1)t^{\alpha - 2} \, dt \qquad \text{and} \qquad v = \int e^{-t} \, dt = -e^{-t}

Applying integration by parts:\Gamma(\alpha) = \underbrace{\left[t^{\alpha-1} \cdot (-e^{-t})\right]_0^{\infty}}_{\text{boundary term}} + (\alpha - 1)\int_0^{\infty} t^{\alpha-2} e^{-t} \, dt

Evaluating the boundary term: We need \lim_{t \to \infty} t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t} and the value at t = 0.

As t \to \infty: the exponential e^{-t} decays to zero faster than any polynomial t^{\alpha-1} grows (this is a standard calculus fact: exponentials always beat polynomials). So \lim_{t \to \infty} t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t} = 0.

At t = 0: 0^{\alpha-1} \cdot e^{0} = 0 \cdot 1 = 0 (since \alpha > 1 means \alpha - 1 > 0).

The boundary term is 0 - 0 = 0. Therefore:\Gamma(\alpha) = 0 + (\alpha - 1) \int_0^{\infty} t^{\alpha-2} e^{-t} \, dt = (\alpha - 1) \cdot \Gamma(\alpha - 1) \qquad \blacksquare

Proof of Property 3: \Gamma(1) = \int_0^{\infty} t^{1-1}e^{-t} \, dt = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-t} \, dt = \left[-e^{-t}\right]_0^{\infty} = 0 - (-1) = 1.

Proof of Property 2 (by induction): From Properties 1 and 3:\Gamma(2) = 1 \cdot \Gamma(1) = 1 = 1!\Gamma(3) = 2 \cdot \Gamma(2) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2!\Gamma(4) = 3 \cdot \Gamma(3) = 3 \cdot 2 = 6 = 3!

In general: \Gamma(n) = (n-1) \cdot (n-2) \cdots 2 \cdot 1 = (n-1)! for any positive integer n.# Verify Gamma function properties
gamma(1)      # 1  (= 0!)
gamma(2)      # 1  (= 1!)
gamma(5)      # 24 (= 4!)
gamma(0.5)    # 1.7724539 (= sqrt(pi))
sqrt(pi)      # 1.7724539 ✓
gamma(10)     # 362880 (= 9!)
factorial(9)  # 362880 ✓

records.content:
Definition 5.11: The Gamma Distribution

A random variable Y has a Gamma distribution with shape parameter \alpha > 0 and scale parameter \beta > 0, written Y \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta), if and only if:f(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y^{\alpha-1} e^{-y/\beta}}{\beta^{\alpha} \, \Gamma(\alpha)}, & y > 0 \\[8pt] 0, & y \leq 0 \end{cases}

The density is zero for y \leq 0 (the Gamma distribution lives on the positive real line), and the denominator \beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha) is the normalizing constant that makes the total area 1.

Verification that \int_0^{\infty} f(y) \, dy = 1:

📐 Calculus Flashback: u-Substitution

To evaluate \int f(g(x)) \cdot g'(x) \, dx, substitute u = g(x), so du = g'(x) \, dx. The integral becomes \int f(u) \, du, which is often simpler. Don’t forget to change the limits if it’s a definite integral.

We need to show \int_0^{\infty} \frac{y^{\alpha-1}e^{-y/\beta}}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \, dy = 1. Substitute u = y/\beta:

If u = y/\beta, then y = u\beta and dy = \beta \, du

When y = 0: u = 0. When y \to \infty: u \to \infty. (Limits don’t change their form.)

Substituting piece by piece:\int_0^{\infty} \frac{y^{\alpha-1} e^{-y/\beta}}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \, dy = \frac{1}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^{\infty} \underbrace{(u\beta)^{\alpha-1}}_{y^{\alpha-1}} \cdot \underbrace{e^{-u}}_{e^{-y/\beta}} \cdot \underbrace{\beta \, du}_{dy}

Now expand (u\beta)^{\alpha-1} = u^{\alpha-1} \cdot \beta^{\alpha-1}, and combine with the extra \beta from dy:= \frac{1}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \cdot \beta^{\alpha-1} \cdot \beta \int_0^{\infty} u^{\alpha-1}e^{-u} \, du = \frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^{\infty} u^{\alpha-1}e^{-u} \, du

The remaining integral is exactly \Gamma(\alpha) by definition:= \frac{\cancel{\beta^{\alpha}}}{\cancel{\beta^{\alpha}}} \cdot \frac{\cancel{\Gamma(\alpha)}}{\cancel{\Gamma(\alpha)}} = 1 \qquad \checkmark

This substitution trick — replacing y/\beta with u to convert a Gamma integral into the definition of \Gamma(\alpha) — will appear repeatedly throughout this chapter and in Section 5.8.

Theorem 5.11: Mean and Variance of the Gamma Distribution

If Y \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta), then:E(Y) = \alpha\beta \qquad \text{and} \qquad V(Y) = \alpha\beta^2

The proof via the moment generating function is given in Section 5.8.# See how the Gamma shape changes with alpha
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (a in c(1, 2, 5, 10)) {
  curve(dgamma(x, shape = a, scale = 2), from = 0, to = 40, lwd = 2,
        main = bquote(alpha == .(a) ~ ", " ~ beta == 2),
        xlab = "y", ylab = "f(y)", col = "steelblue")
  abline(v = a * 2, lty = 2, col = "red")  # mean
}

Run this code and notice: when \alpha = 1, the density is a decreasing exponential. As \alpha increases, the density becomes more bell-shaped and shifts to the right. The red dashed line marks the mean \alpha\beta. The Gamma distribution is remarkably flexible.

records.content:
Definition 5.12: The Exponential Distribution

A random variable Y has an Exponential distribution with scale parameter \beta > 0, written Y \sim \text{Exponential}(\beta), if Y \sim \text{Gamma}(1, \beta). Its density simplifies to:f(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{\beta} e^{-y/\beta}, & y > 0 \\[6pt] 0, & y \leq 0 \end{cases}

Equivalently, with rate parameter \lambda = 1/\beta: f(y) = \lambda e^{-\lambda y} for y > 0.

Since \alpha = 1: E(Y) = \beta = 1/\lambda and V(Y) = \beta^2 = 1/\lambda^2.

The CDF has a closed form (unusual for the Gamma family). Let’s derive it step by step:F(y) = \int_0^y \frac{1}{\beta}e^{-t/\beta} \, dt

📐 Calculus Flashback: Integrating e^{at}\int e^{at} \, dt = \frac{1}{a}e^{at} + C

Here a = -1/\beta, so \int e^{-t/\beta} \, dt = \frac{1}{-1/\beta} e^{-t/\beta} = -\beta \, e^{-t/\beta} + C.F(y) = \frac{1}{\beta} \cdot \left(-\beta \, e^{-t/\beta}\right)\bigg|_0^y = -e^{-t/\beta}\bigg|_0^y = -e^{-y/\beta} - (-e^{0}) = 1 - e^{-y/\beta}

So the Exponential CDF is:F(y) = 1 - e^{-y/\beta}, \qquad y > 0

This is one of the few distributions where the CDF has a clean closed form — no tables or software needed.

records.content:
The Exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with this remarkable property:

Theorem 5.12: Memoryless Property of the Exponential

If Y \sim \text{Exponential}(\beta), then for any s, t > 0:P(Y > s + t \mid Y > s) = P(Y > t)

In words: Given that you’ve already waited s units of time, the probability of waiting at least t more is the same as if you’d just started waiting. The distribution “forgets” how long you’ve been waiting.

Proof.

Strategy: Use the definition of conditional probability and the exponential survival function P(Y > y) = e^{-y/\beta}.P(Y > s + t \mid Y > s) = \frac{P(Y > s + t \text{ and } Y > s)}{P(Y > s)} = \frac{P(Y > s + t)}{P(Y > s)}= \frac{e^{-(s+t)/\beta}}{e^{-s/\beta}} = e^{-t/\beta} = P(Y > t) \qquad \blacksquare

Why this matters: The memoryless property is why the Exponential distribution models the waiting time between Poisson events. If calls arrive at a switchboard according to a Poisson process, the time until the next call is Exponential — and no matter how long you’ve been waiting, the distribution of your remaining wait is the same.

records.content:
There is a deep link between two distributions from different chapters:

The Poisson–Exponential Duality

If events occur according to a Poisson process with rate \lambda events per unit time, then:

The number of events in a time interval of length t follows a \text{Poisson}(\lambda t) distribution (Chapter 4).

The time between consecutive events follows an \text{Exponential}(1/\lambda) distribution.

These are two views of the same random process — one counts events, the other measures gaps.

EXAMPLE 5.12: Exponential Distribution — Transistor Lifetimes

The Problem.

Under harsh operating conditions, the lifetime (in months) of a transistor is Exponentially distributed with parameter \beta = 5 (mean lifetime = 5 months).

(a) Find the probability that the transistor lasts longer than 8 months.

(b) Find the probability that the lifetime is between 3 and 7 months.

(c) Find the median lifetime.

(d) Given that a transistor has survived 6 months, find the probability it survives at least 2 more months.

Solution.

Y \sim \text{Exponential}(\beta = 5), so f(y) = \frac{1}{5}e^{-y/5} and F(y) = 1 - e^{-y/5}.

(a) P(Y > 8) = e^{-8/5} = e^{-1.6} \approx 0.2019

(b) P(3 < Y < 7) = F(7) - F(3) = (1 - e^{-7/5}) - (1 - e^{-3/5}) = e^{-0.6} - e^{-1.4} = 0.5488 - 0.2466 = 0.3022

(c) Solve F(\phi_{0.5}) = 0.5: 1 - e^{-\phi_{0.5}/5} = 0.5 \implies e^{-\phi_{0.5}/5} = 0.5 \implies \phi_{0.5} = -5\ln(0.5) = 5\ln(2) \approx 3.466 months.

The median (3.47 months) is less than the mean (5 months) — the Exponential distribution is heavily right-skewed.

(d) By the memoryless property:P(Y > 8 \mid Y > 6) = P(Y > 2) = e^{-2/5} = e^{-0.4} \approx 0.6703

No calculation involving the 6 months of past survival is needed — the distribution doesn’t “remember.”

In R.# Y ~ Exponential(beta = 5), or equivalently rate = 1/5
# (a) P(Y > 8)
pexp(8, rate = 1/5, lower.tail = FALSE)  # 0.2019

# (b) P(3 < Y < 7)
pexp(7, rate = 1/5) - pexp(3, rate = 1/5)  # 0.3022

# (c) Median
qexp(0.5, rate = 1/5)  # 3.466

# (d) Memoryless: P(Y > 2)
pexp(2, rate = 1/5, lower.tail = FALSE)  # 0.6703

EXAMPLE 5.13: Poisson–Exponential Connection

The Problem.

A radioactive source emits particles according to a Poisson process at a mean rate of 3 particles per second. Let T be the waiting time (in seconds) between consecutive emissions.

(a) What is the distribution of T? Find its mean and standard deviation.

(b) Find P(T > 1).

(c) Find P(0.2 < T < 0.8).

(d) If 2 seconds have elapsed since the last emission, what is the probability that the next emission occurs within 0.5 seconds?

Solution.

The Poisson rate is \lambda = 3 per second, so T \sim \text{Exponential}(\beta = 1/3), or equivalently rate = 3.

(a) E(T) = 1/\lambda = 1/3 seconds, \sigma = 1/\lambda = 1/3 seconds. (For the Exponential, the mean and SD are always equal.)

(b) P(T > 1) = e^{-3(1)} = e^{-3} \approx 0.0498

(c) P(0.2 < T < 0.8) = e^{-3(0.2)} - e^{-3(0.8)} = e^{-0.6} - e^{-2.4} = 0.5488 - 0.0907 = 0.4581

(d) Memoryless property: P(T \leq 2.5 \mid T > 2) = P(T \leq 0.5) = 1 - e^{-3(0.5)} = 1 - e^{-1.5} \approx 0.7769.

The 2 seconds of waiting are irrelevant.

records.content:
Definition 5.13: The Chi-Square Distribution

A random variable Y has a Chi-Square distribution with \nu degrees of freedom, written Y \sim \chi^2(\nu), if Y \sim \text{Gamma}(\nu/2, 2). Its density is:f(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{y^{\nu/2 - 1} e^{-y/2}}{2^{\nu/2} \, \Gamma(\nu/2)}, & y > 0 \\[8pt] 0, & y \leq 0 \end{cases}

Since \alpha = \nu/2 and \beta = 2: E(Y) = \nu and V(Y) = 2\nu.

Why does the Chi-Square matter? If Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_\nu are independent standard Normal random variables, then:Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + \cdots + Z_\nu^2 \sim \chi^2(\nu)

This is the bridge between the Normal distribution and statistical inference. In mathematical statistics, the Chi-Square distribution is used for testing hypotheses about variances, goodness-of-fit tests, and constructing confidence intervals.# Visualize the Gamma family tree
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

# Exponential: Gamma(1, 2)
curve(dgamma(x, 1, scale = 2), 0, 15, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
      main = "Exponential(β=2)\n= Gamma(1, 2)", ylab = "f(y)")

# Chi-Square(6): Gamma(3, 2)
curve(dgamma(x, 3, scale = 2), 0, 25, lwd = 2, col = "darkorange",
      main = "Chi-Square(ν=6)\n= Gamma(3, 2)", ylab = "f(y)")

# General Gamma(5, 3)
curve(dgamma(x, 5, scale = 3), 0, 40, lwd = 2, col = "purple",
      main = "Gamma(α=5, β=3)", ylab = "f(y)")

EXAMPLE 5.14: General Gamma Distribution

The Problem.

The time (in minutes) a randomly selected student spends using a computer terminal has a Gamma distribution with mean 20 minutes and variance 80 min^2.

(a) Find the parameters \alpha and \beta.

(b) Find the probability that a student uses the terminal for at most 24 minutes.

(c) Find the probability that a student uses it between 15 and 30 minutes.

Solution.

(a) From the mean and variance formulas:\alpha\beta = 20 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \alpha\beta^2 = 80

Dividing the second by the first: \beta = 80/20 = 4. Then \alpha = 20/4 = 5.

So Y \sim \text{Gamma}(5, 4).

(b) There is no closed-form CDF for the general Gamma distribution (except when \alpha is a positive integer, via integration by parts). We use R:# Y ~ Gamma(shape = 5, scale = 4)
pgamma(24, shape = 5, scale = 4)  # 0.7149

P(Y \leq 24) \approx 0.715.

(c) P(15 \leq Y \leq 30) = F(30) - F(15):pgamma(30, shape = 5, scale = 4) - pgamma(15, shape = 5, scale = 4)
# 0.5455

About 55% of students spend between 15 and 30 minutes.

Interpretation.

To find \alpha and \beta from the mean and variance, always use the same trick: divide V(Y) = \alpha\beta^2 by E(Y) = \alpha\beta to get \beta, then solve for \alpha. This works because the \alpha cancels cleanly.

Guided Practice 5.5: Identifying and using Gamma family distributions

Solution.

A random variable Y has the density function:f(y) = \begin{cases} k \, y^3 \, e^{-y/2}, & y > 0 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}

(a) Identify the distribution by matching to the Gamma density.

Compare with the Gamma density: f(y) = \frac{y^{\alpha-1}e^{-y/\beta}}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)}.

Exponent of y: 3 = \alpha - 1 \implies \alpha = 4

Exponent of e: -y/2 \implies \beta = 2

So Y \sim \text{Gamma}(4, 2), which is also \chi^2(8) (since \alpha = \nu/2 = 4 \implies \nu = 8, and \beta = 2).

(b) Find k.k = \frac{1}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} = \frac{1}{2^4 \cdot \Gamma(4)} = \frac{1}{16 \cdot 6} = \frac{1}{96}

(c) Find E(Y) and V(Y).E(Y) = \alpha\beta = 4(2) = 8 \qquad V(Y) = \alpha\beta^2 = 4(4) = 16

Or, since Y \sim \chi^2(8): E(Y) = \nu = 8 and V(Y) = 2\nu = 16 ✓.

(d) Find P(Y > 12).pgamma(12, shape = 4, scale = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)  # 0.1512
# Equivalently:
pchisq(12, df = 8, lower.tail = FALSE)  # 0.1512  ✓

records.content:
5.6.1. The time (in hours) until a server crashes follows an Exponential distribution with mean 200 hours.

(a) Find the probability that the server runs for at least 300 hours without crashing.
(b) Given that it has run for 150 hours, find the probability it runs at least 100 more hours.
(c) What is the median time to failure?
(d) Find the probability that the server crashes within the first 50 hours.

5.6.2. Calls arrive at a helpline at a Poisson rate of 4 per hour. Let T be the time (in hours) between consecutive calls.

(a) What is the distribution of T? State its mean and variance.
(b) Find P(T > 0.5).
(c) Find P(T < 0.1).
(d) A new operator is told “on average, you’ll wait 15 minutes between calls.” Verify this claim.

5.6.3. A random variable Y has the density:f(y) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{6}y \, e^{-y/3}, & y > 0 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}

(a) Identify the Gamma parameters \alpha and \beta.
(b) Find E(Y) and \sigma.
(c) Find P(Y > 10) using R.

5.6.4. A Chi-Square random variable has 12 degrees of freedom.

(a) State the mean and variance.
(b) Express this as a Gamma distribution.
(c) Use R to find P(\chi^2_{12} > 21.026). What significance does this value have?

5.6.5. (Proof) Prove the memoryless property of the Exponential distribution: if Y \sim \text{Exp}(\beta), then P(Y > s + t \mid Y > s) = P(Y > t) for all s, t > 0. Then show that if Y has a non-Exponential continuous distribution supported on (0, \infty), the memoryless property fails. (Hint: For the second part, consider a specific counterexample such as the Gamma(2, 1) distribution.)

5.6.6. Show that \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}. (Hint: Write \Gamma(1/2) = \int_0^{\infty} t^{-1/2}e^{-t} \, dt, make the substitution t = u^2/2, and recognize the resulting integral as related to the standard Normal density.)

⚠️ Common Mistakes — The Gamma Family

Confusing scale \beta with rate \lambda = 1/\beta. Some textbooks (and R’s dexp function) parameterize the Exponential by the rate \lambda. This book (and the reference textbook) use the scale \beta = 1/\lambda. In R: dexp(y, rate = lambda) = dgamma(y, shape = 1, scale = 1/lambda). Always check which convention your source uses.

Forgetting that \Gamma(n) = (n-1)!, not n!. The Gamma function is “shifted” by one compared to the factorial: \Gamma(5) = 4! = 24, not 5! = 120.

Trying to find a closed-form CDF for the general Gamma. There is no closed-form CDF when \alpha is not a positive integer. Use R’s pgamma() or tables. The Exponential (\alpha = 1) is the exception — its CDF is 1 - e^{-y/\beta}.

Applying the memoryless property to non-Exponential distributions. Only the Exponential distribution (among continuous distributions) is memoryless. If a component’s lifetime is Gamma(2, 5) instead of Exponential(5), the conditional probability P(Y > s+t \mid Y > s) \neq P(Y > t). Don’t assume memorylessness without checking that \alpha = 1.

Mixing up Chi-Square parameters. The \chi^2(\nu) distribution has E(Y) = \nu and V(Y) = 2\nu. Students sometimes write V(Y) = \nu or E(Y) = 2\nu. Remember: the variance is twice the mean.

🔬 What Did We Learn?

The Gamma distribution is a flexible, right-skewed family defined by shape \alpha and scale \beta. It lives on (0, \infty) and has mean \alpha\beta and variance \alpha\beta^2. Two critically important distributions are special cases:

Exponential (\alpha = 1): models wait times between Poisson events, has the memoryless property, and has a closed-form CDF F(y) = 1 - e^{-y/\beta}.

Chi-Square (\alpha = \nu/2, \beta = 2): the sum of \nu squared standard Normals, with mean \nu and variance 2\nu.

The real-life interpretation: The Exponential distribution governs “waiting for the next event” — the next call, the next failure, the next emission. Its memoryless property is both mathematically elegant and practically useful: if a component’s lifetime is truly Exponential, then a 5-year-old component is just as likely to fail tomorrow as a brand-new one. This is why the Exponential models random failure (like a light bulb burning out) but not wear-out failure (like brake pads wearing thin). For wear-out, you need a Gamma with \alpha > 1 — a distribution that “remembers” how long the component has been in use.

The Gamma function \Gamma(\alpha) is the mathematical glue holding the family together, extending the factorial to non-integer values and serving as the normalizing constant for the Gamma density.

Looking ahead: The Beta distribution (Section 5.7) is the next named distribution — it models proportions and percentages, living on the interval [0, 1] rather than on (0, \infty).

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

All the distributions so far live on infinite or semi-infinite intervals: the Normal on (-\infty, \infty), the Gamma on (0, \infty), the Uniform on any finite interval. But what if your random variable is a proportion — a number that must lie between 0 and 1?

The proportion of defective items in a shipment. The fraction of the day a machine is running. A baseball player’s batting average. A website’s click-through rate. All are numbers between 0 and 1, and the Beta distribution is designed specifically to model them.

The Beta distribution has two shape parameters, \alpha and \beta, that control whether the density is U-shaped, bell-shaped, left-skewed, right-skewed, or flat. When \alpha = \beta = 1, it reduces to the Uniform(0, 1) — so the Uniform is actually a special case of the Beta.

Real-life motivation: A factory’s weekly repair cost, expressed as a fraction of the total budget, follows a Beta distribution. If \alpha and \beta are known, management can answer: “What is the probability that repairs consume more than 40% of our budget this week?” That’s a Beta probability.

Theorem 5.13: Mean and Variance of the Beta Distribution

If Y \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta), then:E(Y) = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + \beta} \qquad \text{and} \qquad V(Y) = \frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha + \beta)^2(\alpha + \beta + 1)}

Proof of E(Y).

Strategy: Integrate y \cdot f(y) over [0, 1], then recognize the result as a ratio of Beta functions.E(Y) = \int_0^1 y \cdot \frac{y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)} \, dy = \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} \int_0^1 y^{\alpha}(1-y)^{\beta-1} \, dy

The integral \int_0^1 y^{\alpha}(1-y)^{\beta-1} \, dy has the form \int_0^1 y^{(\alpha+1)-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1} \, dy = B(\alpha+1, \beta). So:E(Y) = \frac{B(\alpha+1, \beta)}{B(\alpha, \beta)} = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}

The \Gamma(\beta) terms cancel. Using the recursion \Gamma(\alpha+1) = \alpha \cdot \Gamma(\alpha) and \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1) = (\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta):= \frac{\alpha \cdot \cancel{\Gamma(\alpha)} \cdot \cancel{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}}{\cancel{\Gamma(\alpha)} \cdot (\alpha+\beta) \cdot \cancel{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + \beta} \qquad \blacksquare

The variance proof follows the same pattern (computing E(Y^2) via B(\alpha+2, \beta)/B(\alpha, \beta) and applying the shortcut formula). We leave the detailed algebra as Exercise 5.7.5.

\alpha = \beta = 1: f(y) = 1 — the \text{Uniform}(0, 1)

\alpha = \beta > 1: symmetric, bell-shaped, centered at 1/2

\alpha > \beta: left-skewed (piles up near 1)

\alpha < \beta: right-skewed (piles up near 0)

\alpha < 1 and \beta < 1: U-shaped (concentrated near 0 and 1)# Visualize the Beta family's flexibility

EXAMPLE 5.15: Weekly Repair Costs

The Problem.

The weekly repair cost Y for a machine, measured as a proportion of the weekly budget, has the density:f(y) = \begin{cases} 6y(1 - y), & 0 \leq y \leq 1 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere} \end{cases}

(a) Identify the distribution.

(b) Find E(Y) and V(Y).

(c) Find the probability that repair costs exceed 60% of the budget.

(d) How much should be budgeted so actual costs exceed the budget only 10% of the time?

Solution.

(a) Compare f(y) = 6y(1 - y) = 6 y^{2-1}(1-y)^{2-1} with the Beta density. We identify \alpha = 2, \beta = 2, and the constant is 6 = 1/B(2,2) = \Gamma(4)/[\Gamma(2)\Gamma(2)] = 6/(1 \cdot 1) = 6 ✓.

So Y \sim \text{Beta}(2, 2).

(b) Using the formulas:E(Y) = \frac{2}{2+2} = \frac{1}{2} = 0.50V(Y) = \frac{2 \cdot 2}{(2+2)^2(2+2+1)} = \frac{4}{16 \cdot 5} = \frac{4}{80} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05\sigma = \sqrt{0.05} \approx 0.2236

(c) P(Y > 0.6) = \int_{0.6}^{1} 6y(1-y) \, dy

Using the power rule: 6y(1-y) = 6y - 6y^2= \int_{0.6}^{1} (6y - 6y^2) \, dy = \left[3y^2 - 2y^3\right]_{0.6}^{1} = (3 - 2) - (3(0.36) - 2(0.216)) = 1 - (1.08 - 0.432) = 1 - 0.648 = 0.352

About 35.2% of weeks, costs exceed 60% of the budget.

(d) Find c such that P(Y > c) = 0.10, i.e., P(Y \leq c) = 0.90:qbeta(0.90, 2, 2)  # 0.8042

Budget about 80.4% of the maximum to keep overruns below 10%.

Guided Practice 5.6: Recognizing and using the Beta distribution

Solution.

During an eight-hour shift, the proportion of time Y a stamping machine is down for maintenance has a \text{Beta}(1, 2) distribution.

(a) Write down the PDF.

With \alpha = 1, \beta = 2: B(1,2) = \Gamma(1)\Gamma(2)/\Gamma(3) = (1)(1)/(2) = 1/2.f(y) = \frac{y^{0}(1-y)^{1}}{1/2} = 2(1-y), \qquad 0 \leq y \leq 1

(b) Find E(Y) and V(Y).E(Y) = \frac{1}{1+2} = \frac{1}{3} \qquad V(Y) = \frac{1 \cdot 2}{(3)^2(4)} = \frac{2}{36} = \frac{1}{18}

(c) The cost of downtime is C = 10 + 20Y + 4Y^2. Find E(C).

We need E(Y^2) = V(Y) + [E(Y)]^2 = 1/18 + 1/9 = 1/18 + 2/18 = 3/18 = 1/6.E(C) = 10 + 20 \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 4 \cdot \frac{1}{6} = 10 + \frac{20}{3} + \frac{2}{3} = 10 + \frac{22}{3} = \frac{52}{3} \approx \$17.33

🔬 What Did We Learn?

The Beta distribution models random proportions on [0, 1], with density f(y) \propto y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}. Its two parameters give it extraordinary flexibility: symmetric or skewed, bell-shaped or U-shaped, concentrated or spread out.

The real-life interpretation: Any time you have a random variable that is naturally a fraction or percentage — market share, completion rate, defect rate, the proportion of a budget consumed — the Beta distribution is a natural candidate. Its mean \alpha/(\alpha + \beta) is a “weighted average” of 0 and 1, where \alpha represents “successes” and \beta represents “failures.” In Bayesian statistics (which you’ll meet in mathematical statistics), the Beta distribution is the standard prior for unknown probabilities.

Looking ahead: Section 5.8 introduces moment generating functions for continuous distributions — the tool that lets us prove the mean and variance formulas for the Normal and Gamma distributions, and provides a powerful method for identifying distributions.

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

In Chapter 4, we introduced moment generating functions (MGFs) for discrete random variables. The idea was simple but powerful: if you can find M(t) = E(e^{tY}), then the kth moment E(Y^k) is the kth derivative M^{(k)}(0).

Now we extend MGFs to continuous distributions. The definition is the same — only the computation changes from a sum to an integral. We’ll use MGFs to prove the mean and variance formulas for the Normal and Gamma distributions that we stated without proof in earlier sections.

MGFs also have a uniqueness property: if two distributions have the same MGF, they are the same distribution. This means MGFs serve as “fingerprints” — you can identify a distribution by computing its MGF and matching it to a known form.

Real-life motivation: Suppose you know a random variable has MGF M(t) = (1 - 2t)^{-3}. Without any other information, you can conclude it’s a \text{Gamma}(3, 2) distribution (or equivalently, a \chi^2(6)). The MGF uniquely identifies the distribution.

records.content:
Before the MGF, let us formally define moments — a concept also covered in the reference textbook (Definition 4.13).

Definition 5.15a: Moments of a Continuous Random Variable

If Y is a continuous random variable, the kth moment about the origin (or kth raw moment) is:\mu_k' = E(Y^k) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y^k f(y) \, dy, \qquad k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots

The kth moment about the mean (or kth central moment) is:\mu_k = E[(Y - \mu)^k], \qquad k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots

Notice that \mu_1' = \mu = E(Y) (the mean) and \mu_2 = V(Y) = \sigma^2 (the variance). The third central moment \mu_3 measures skewness, and the fourth \mu_4 measures kurtosis (tail heaviness).

Definition 5.15: Moment-Generating Function (Continuous)

The moment-generating function of a continuous random variable Y is:M(t) = E(e^{tY}) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{ty} f(y) \, dy

provided the integral exists for all t in some interval (-h, h) around 0.

Theorem 5.14: Moments from the MGF

If M(t) exists, then the kth moment of Y is:E(Y^k) = M^{(k)}(0) = \frac{d^k M(t)}{dt^k}\bigg|_{t=0}

In particular: E(Y) = M'(0) and E(Y^2) = M''(0).

records.content:
This is the most important MGF derivation in this chapter, because it also gives us the Exponential and Chi-Square MGFs as special cases.

Theorem 5.15: MGF of the Gamma Distribution

If Y \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta), then:M(t) = (1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha}, \qquad t < 1/\beta

Proof.

Strategy: Compute E(e^{tY}) by integrating, then use the same substitution trick from the Gamma normalization proof to convert the integral into a recognizable \Gamma(\alpha) form.M(t) = E(e^{tY}) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{ty} \cdot \frac{y^{\alpha-1}e^{-y/\beta}}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \, dy

Combine the two exponentials: e^{ty} \cdot e^{-y/\beta} = e^{y(t - 1/\beta)} = e^{-y(1/\beta - t)}.

For this integral to converge, we need 1/\beta - t > 0, i.e., t < 1/\beta. Assuming this:M(t) = \frac{1}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^{\infty} y^{\alpha-1} e^{-y(1/\beta - t)} \, dy

📐 Calculus Flashback: u-Substitution for This Integral

Let u = y(1/\beta - t), so y = u/(1/\beta - t) and dy = du/(1/\beta - t).

When y = 0: u = 0. When y \to \infty: u \to \infty.

Write 1/\beta - t = (1 - \beta t)/\beta to keep expressions clean.

Substitute u = y \cdot \frac{1 - \beta t}{\beta}, so y = \frac{u\beta}{1 - \beta t} and dy = \frac{\beta}{1 - \beta t} \, du:M(t) = \frac{1}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^{\infty} \left(\frac{u\beta}{1-\beta t}\right)^{\alpha-1} e^{-u} \cdot \frac{\beta}{1-\beta t} \, du

Collect the powers of \beta/(1-\beta t): the exponent \alpha - 1 from the y^{\alpha-1} term plus 1 from the dy term gives \alpha total:= \frac{1}{\beta^{\alpha}\Gamma(\alpha)} \cdot \frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{(1-\beta t)^{\alpha}} \int_0^{\infty} u^{\alpha-1}e^{-u} \, du

The \beta^{\alpha} terms cancel. The integral is \Gamma(\alpha):= \frac{\cancel{\beta^{\alpha}}}{\cancel{\beta^{\alpha}} \cdot \cancel{\Gamma(\alpha)}} \cdot \frac{\cancel{\Gamma(\alpha)}}{(1-\beta t)^{\alpha}} = (1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha} \qquad \blacksquare

Now we can finally prove Theorem 5.11:M(t) = (1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha}

First derivative (using the chain rule: \frac{d}{dt}(1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha} = -\alpha(1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha - 1} \cdot (-\beta) = \alpha\beta(1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha - 1}):M'(t) = \alpha\beta(1 - \beta t)^{-\alpha-1}E(Y) = M'(0) = \alpha\beta(1)^{-\alpha-1} = \alpha\beta \qquad \checkmark

Second derivative (chain rule again):M''(t) = \alpha\beta \cdot (-\alpha-1)(1-\beta t)^{-\alpha-2} \cdot (-\beta) = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2(1-\beta t)^{-\alpha-2}E(Y^2) = M''(0) = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2

Variance:V(Y) = E(Y^2) - [E(Y)]^2 = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2 - (\alpha\beta)^2 = \alpha^2\beta^2 + \alpha\beta^2 - \alpha^2\beta^2 = \alpha\beta^2 \qquad \checkmark

records.content:
Theorem 5.16: MGF of the Normal Distribution

If Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), then:M(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2 / 2}

Proof.

Strategy: Start with the standard Normal (\mu = 0, \sigma = 1), then generalize using Y = \mu + \sigma Z.

Step 1: Standard Normal MGF. For Z \sim N(0, 1):M_Z(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{tz} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2} \, dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{tz - z^2/2} \, dz

The key trick is completing the square in the exponent:tz - \frac{z^2}{2} = -\frac{1}{2}(z^2 - 2tz) = -\frac{1}{2}(z^2 - 2tz + t^2) + \frac{t^2}{2} = -\frac{(z-t)^2}{2} + \frac{t^2}{2}

📐 Calculus Flashback: Completing the Square

To rewrite az^2 + bz + c as a(z - h)^2 + k: factor out a, then add and subtract (b/2a)^2 inside the parentheses. Here: z^2 - 2tz = (z - t)^2 - t^2.

So:M_Z(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{t^2/2} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-(z-t)^2/2} \, dz

The remaining integral is the total area under a N(t, 1) density (shifted Normal), which equals \sqrt{2\pi}. Therefore:M_Z(t) = \frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{2\pi}}} \cdot e^{t^2/2} \cdot \cancel{\sqrt{2\pi}} = e^{t^2/2}

Step 2: General Normal. If Y = \mu + \sigma Z, then E(e^{tY}) = E(e^{t(\mu + \sigma Z)}) = e^{t\mu} \cdot E(e^{(t\sigma)Z}) = e^{t\mu} \cdot e^{(t\sigma)^2/2} = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \qquad \blacksquare

Deriving E(Y) and V(Y) from the Normal MGF:M'(t) = (\mu + \sigma^2 t) \cdot e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \implies E(Y) = M'(0) = \mu \cdot 1 = \mu \qquad \checkmarkM''(t) = [\sigma^2 + (\mu + \sigma^2 t)^2] \cdot e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \implies E(Y^2) = M''(0) = \sigma^2 + \mu^2V(Y) = (\sigma^2 + \mu^2) - \mu^2 = \sigma^2 \qquad \checkmark

5.8.2. A random variable has MGF M(t) = (1 - 4t)^{-3}. Identify the distribution, and state its mean and variance.

5.8.3. A random variable has MGF M(t) = e^{5t + 8t^2}. Identify the distribution, and state its mean and variance.

5.8.4. (Proof) Using the Gamma MGF, prove that the sum of \nu independent Exponential(\beta) random variables has a \text{Gamma}(\nu, \beta) distribution. (Hint: The MGF of a sum of independent RVs is the product of their individual MGFs. What is [(1-\beta t)^{-1}]^{\nu}?)

🔬 What Did We Learn?

The moment generating function M(t) = E(e^{tY}) is a powerful tool with three uses:

Finding moments: E(Y) = M'(0), E(Y^2) = M''(0), then V(Y) = M''(0) - [M'(0)]^2.

Proving mean/variance formulas: We used the Gamma MGF (1-\beta t)^{-\alpha} to prove E(Y) = \alpha\beta and V(Y) = \alpha\beta^2, and the Normal MGF e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} to prove E(Y) = \mu and V(Y) = \sigma^2.

Identifying distributions: If you compute an MGF and it matches a known form, you’ve identified the distribution — because MGFs are unique.

The real-life interpretation: MGFs are a theoretical tool, not something you’d compute on the job. But they’re the engine behind many results you’ll use constantly: the fact that a sum of independent Normals is Normal, the fact that a sum of independent Gammas (with the same \beta) is Gamma, and the Central Limit Theorem itself. These are proved using MGFs.

Looking ahead: Our final section gives a universal bound on probabilities — Tchebysheff’s theorem works for any distribution, with no assumptions about its shape.

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

Every distribution we’ve studied — Uniform, Normal, Gamma, Beta — has its own specific formula for computing P(|Y - \mu| \geq k\sigma). But what if you don’t know the distribution? What if all you know is the mean \mu and variance \sigma^2?

Tchebysheff’s theorem gives a universal bound: for any distribution (continuous or discrete), at least 1 - 1/k^2 of the probability lies within k standard deviations of the mean. This bound is conservative — it’s rarely tight — but it works with no assumptions about the shape of the distribution.

Real-life motivation: A quality engineer knows a part has mean diameter \mu = 10 mm and standard deviation \sigma = 0.3 mm, but doesn’t know the exact distribution. Tchebysheff guarantees that at least 75% of parts are within \pm 0.6 mm of the mean (k = 2), and at least 89% are within \pm 0.9 mm (k = 3) — regardless of the distribution’s shape.

Theorem 5.17: Tchebysheff’s Theorem (Continuous Version)

Let Y be a continuous random variable with mean \mu and finite variance \sigma^2. Then for any k > 0:P(|Y - \mu| \geq k\sigma) \leq \frac{1}{k^2}

Equivalently: P(|Y - \mu| < k\sigma) \geq 1 - \frac{1}{k^2}

Proof.

Strategy: Start from the definition of variance and cleverly restrict the domain of integration to show that the variance is at least as large as k^2\sigma^2 times the probability we want to bound.\sigma^2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (y - \mu)^2 f(y) \, dy

This integral is over all y. Since the integrand (y-\mu)^2 f(y) is nonnegative everywhere, the integral over all of \mathbb{R} is at least as large as the integral over any subset. In particular, restricting to the set where |y - \mu| \geq k\sigma:\sigma^2 \geq \int_{|y - \mu| \geq k\sigma} (y - \mu)^2 f(y) \, dy

On this restricted domain, |y - \mu| \geq k\sigma, which means (y - \mu)^2 \geq k^2\sigma^2. Replace the integrand with this lower bound:\geq \int_{|y - \mu| \geq k\sigma} k^2\sigma^2 \, f(y) \, dy = k^2\sigma^2 \int_{|y - \mu| \geq k\sigma} f(y) \, dy = k^2\sigma^2 \cdot P(|Y - \mu| \geq k\sigma)

So \sigma^2 \geq k^2\sigma^2 \cdot P(|Y - \mu| \geq k\sigma). Divide both sides by k^2\sigma^2:P(|Y - \mu| \geq k\sigma) \leq \frac{1}{k^2} \qquad \blacksquare

Standard values:

k

At most 1/k^2 outside \mu \pm k\sigma

At least 1 - 1/k^2 inside

2

\leq 25\%

\geq 75\%

3

\leq 11.1\%

\geq 88.9\%

4

\leq 6.25\%

\geq 93.75\%

Compare these to the Normal: for k=2, the Normal has 4.56% outside (not 25%), and for k=3, only 0.27% (not 11.1%). Tchebysheff is conservative — but it works for every distribution, not just the Normal.

EXAMPLE 5.16: Tchebysheff Applied to an Unknown Distribution

The Problem.

Experience shows that the time (in minutes) for a periodic maintenance check on a machine follows a Gamma distribution with \alpha = 3.1 and \beta = 2. A new maintenance worker takes 22.5 minutes. Does this time disagree with prior experience?

Solution.

\mu = \alpha\beta = 3.1(2) = 6.2 minutes. \sigma^2 = \alpha\beta^2 = 3.1(4) = 12.4, so \sigma = \sqrt{12.4} \approx 3.52.

How far is 22.5 from the mean? |22.5 - 6.2| = 16.3, and k = 16.3/3.52 \approx 4.63.

By Tchebysheff: P(|Y - 6.2| \geq 16.3) \leq 1/4.63^2 \approx 0.047.

There is at most a 4.7% chance of a maintenance time this far from the mean. This suggests the new worker’s time is unusually long — possibly due to inexperience.

We can also compute the exact probability using R:# Exact: P(Y > 22.5) for Gamma(3.1, scale = 2)
pgamma(22.5, shape = 3.1, scale = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
# 0.001150 — much smaller than Tchebysheff's bound of 0.047

The exact probability is about 0.12% — Tchebysheff’s bound of 4.7% is very conservative (as expected), but both tell the same story: this time is unusually long.

🔬 What Did We Learn?

Tchebysheff’s theorem gives a distribution-free bound: for any distribution with finite mean and variance, at least 1 - 1/k^2 of the probability lies within k standard deviations of the mean. It requires no assumptions about symmetry, shape, or tail behavior.

The real-life interpretation: When you don’t know the distribution but you know \mu and \sigma, Tchebysheff gives you a guaranteed minimum. An engineer who knows a component’s average lifetime is 1000 hours with SD 100 hours can guarantee — without knowing the distribution — that at least 75% of components last between 800 and 1200 hours. If the distribution is actually Normal, the true percentage is 95.4%, but 75% is the guaranteed floor.

The bound is conservative because it must hold for all distributions, including the worst-case ones. But conservative guarantees are still guarantees — and in engineering and quality control, guarantees matter.

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

We’ve now learned six named distributions. A natural question: when you encounter a real-world random variable, how do you decide which distribution to use? This optional section gives practical guidance — a decision framework based on the variable’s support, shape, and the context that generated it.

This matches Section 4.8 in the reference textbook (“Some General Comments”) and is worth reading even if your course skips it.

Choosing a distribution is a modeling decision, not a mathematical derivation. No real-world data follows any theoretical distribution exactly — the question is whether the model is useful enough for the inferences you need to make.

Here is a practical guide:

Some distributions are linked to specific physical processes:

Poisson events in time? The count is Poisson, the wait time between events is Exponential, and the wait for the \alphath event is Gamma.

Sum of many small independent effects? The result is approximately Normal (Central Limit Theorem).

Sum of squared standard Normals? The result is Chi-Square.

Measuring a proportion or percentage? Use Beta.

Complete ignorance within a known range? Use Uniform.

As the reference textbook emphasizes: a good model is not one that perfectly matches reality — it is one that yields good inferences about the population of interest. A Normal approximation that’s slightly off in the tails might still produce excellent confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

🔬 What Did We Learn?

Choosing a distribution involves three questions: what values can the variable take (support), what shape does the histogram have, and what physical process generated the data? No model is perfect, but a thoughtfully chosen one supports sound statistical inference — which is the ultimate goal.

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

The Exponential distribution models lifetimes with a constant failure rate — the item is just as likely to fail in the next hour whether it’s brand new or ten years old. But many real-world items wear out: their failure rate increases with age (brake pads, tires, bearings). Others have decreasing failure rates due to early manufacturing defects being weeded out (“infant mortality” in electronics).

The Weibull distribution handles all three cases with a single family. It has a shape parameter \alpha that controls whether the failure rate is decreasing (\alpha < 1), constant (\alpha = 1, which gives the Exponential), or increasing (\alpha > 1). This makes it the most widely used distribution in reliability engineering.

Real-life motivation: An automotive manufacturer needs to set warranty periods for brake pads. The pads wear out faster as they age — a classic increasing failure rate. The Weibull distribution models this perfectly, letting engineers compute “what fraction of brake pads will fail before 50,000 miles?” The reference textbook includes Weibull exercises in its supplementary problems.

records.content:
Definition 5.16: The Weibull Distribution

A random variable Y has a Weibull distribution with shape parameter \alpha > 0 and scale parameter \beta > 0, written Y \sim \text{Weibull}(\alpha, \beta), if and only if:f(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\alpha}{\beta^{\alpha}} y^{\alpha - 1} e^{-(y/\beta)^{\alpha}}, & y > 0 \\[8pt] 0, & y \leq 0 \end{cases}

Connection to the Exponential: When \alpha = 1, the Weibull density becomes f(y) = \frac{1}{\beta}e^{-y/\beta} — exactly the Exponential(\beta) density. So the Exponential is a special case of both the Gamma and the Weibull families.

The CDF has a closed form (just like the Exponential):F(y) = 1 - e^{-(y/\beta)^{\alpha}}, \qquad y > 0

📐 Calculus Flashback: Deriving the Weibull CDF

To integrate f(y) = \frac{\alpha}{\beta^{\alpha}}y^{\alpha-1}e^{-(y/\beta)^{\alpha}}, use the substitution u = (y/\beta)^{\alpha}, so du = \frac{\alpha}{\beta^{\alpha}}y^{\alpha-1} \, dy. The integrand becomes exactly e^{-u} \, du, which integrates to -e^{-u}. Evaluating: F(y) = [-e^{-u}]_0^{(y/\beta)^{\alpha}} = 1 - e^{-(y/\beta)^{\alpha}}.

Theorem 5.18: Mean and Variance of the Weibull Distribution

If Y \sim \text{Weibull}(\alpha, \beta), then:E(Y) = \beta \, \Gamma\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \qquad \text{and} \qquad V(Y) = \beta^2 \left[\Gamma\!\left(1 + \frac{2}{\alpha}\right) - \left(\Gamma\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\right)^2\right]

Proof of E(Y) (sketch).E(Y) = \int_0^{\infty} y \cdot \frac{\alpha}{\beta^{\alpha}}y^{\alpha-1}e^{-(y/\beta)^{\alpha}} \, dy

Substitute u = (y/\beta)^{\alpha}, so y = \beta u^{1/\alpha} and dy = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}u^{1/\alpha - 1} \, du:= \int_0^{\infty} \beta u^{1/\alpha} \cdot e^{-u} \, du = \beta \int_0^{\infty} u^{(1 + 1/\alpha) - 1} e^{-u} \, du = \beta \, \Gamma\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \qquad \blacksquare

Check: When \alpha = 1 (Exponential): E(Y) = \beta \, \Gamma(2) = \beta \cdot 1 = \beta ✓

records.content:
The hazard function (or failure rate) of a distribution is h(y) = f(y) / [1 - F(y)] — the instantaneous risk of failure at time y, given survival to y.

For the Weibull:h(y) = \frac{\alpha}{\beta^{\alpha}} y^{\alpha - 1}

\alpha < 1: h(y) decreases — “infant mortality” (early failures dominate)

\alpha = 1: h(y) = 1/\beta = constant — memoryless (Exponential)

\alpha > 1: h(y) increases — wear-out (aging causes failure)

This is precisely why the Weibull is the workhorse of reliability engineering.# Weibull shapes and hazard functions
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (a in c(0.5, 1, 3)) {
  curve(dweibull(x, shape = a, scale = 2), 0, 5, lwd = 2,
        main = bquote(alpha == .(a)),
        xlab = "y", ylab = "f(y)", col = "steelblue")
}

EXAMPLE 5.17: Weibull Reliability Analysis

The Problem.

The lifetime (in thousands of hours) of a bearing follows a Weibull distribution with \alpha = 2 and \beta = 5.

(a) Find the probability the bearing lasts at least 4,000 hours.

(b) Find the mean lifetime.

(c) Find the median lifetime.

Solution.

(a) Using the closed-form CDF:P(Y > 4) = 1 - F(4) = e^{-(4/5)^2} = e^{-0.64} \approx 0.5273

About 52.7% of bearings last at least 4,000 hours.

(b) E(Y) = 5 \cdot \Gamma(1 + 1/2) = 5 \cdot \Gamma(3/2) = 5 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} \approx 5(0.8862) = 4.431 thousand hours.

📐 Calculus Flashback: \Gamma(3/2)

\Gamma(3/2) = (1/2)\Gamma(1/2) = (1/2)\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.8862 (using the recursion \Gamma(\alpha) = (\alpha-1)\Gamma(\alpha-1)).

(c) Median: solve F(\phi_{0.5}) = 0.5:1 - e^{-(\phi_{0.5}/5)^2} = 0.5 \implies e^{-(\phi_{0.5}/5)^2} = 0.5 \implies (\phi_{0.5}/5)^2 = \ln 2\phi_{0.5} = 5\sqrt{\ln 2} \approx 5(0.8326) = 4.163 \text{ thousand hours}

In R.# Y ~ Weibull(shape = 2, scale = 5)
# (a) P(Y > 4)
pweibull(4, shape = 2, scale = 5, lower.tail = FALSE)  # 0.5273

# (b) Mean
5 * gamma(1 + 1/2)  # 4.4312

# (c) Median
qweibull(0.5, shape = 2, scale = 5)  # 4.1628

🔬 What Did We Learn?

The Weibull distribution generalizes the Exponential by adding a shape parameter \alpha that controls whether failure rates increase, decrease, or remain constant. Its closed-form CDF F(y) = 1 - e^{-(y/\beta)^{\alpha}} makes probability calculations easy. When \alpha = 1, it reduces to the Exponential — memoryless. When \alpha > 1, the failure rate increases with age, modeling wear-out. When \alpha < 1, it decreases — modeling infant mortality in manufactured products.

records.content:
🔭 What Are We About to Learn?

In Chapter 4, we learned the Binomial distribution for counting successes. But computing Binomial probabilities for large n is painful — try evaluating \binom{500}{237} by hand! The Normal approximation to the Binomial saves us: when n is large enough, a \text{Binomial}(n, p) random variable is approximately N(np, np(1-p)).

This is actually a preview of the Central Limit Theorem from Chapter 7, applied to the special case where we’re summing independent Bernoulli trials. The approximation includes a continuity correction to account for the fact that we’re approximating a discrete distribution (integer values) with a continuous one (all real values).

Real-life motivation: A polling firm surveys 1,200 voters. If the true proportion supporting Candidate A is p = 0.52, what’s the probability the poll shows Candidate A with at least 55% support? This is a Binomial problem with n = 1200, but using the Normal approximation makes it a simple Z-score calculation.

records.content:
Theorem 5.19: Normal Approximation to the Binomial

If Y \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p), then for large n:Z = \frac{Y - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}} \approx N(0, 1)

Rule of thumb: The approximation is adequate when np \geq 5 and n(1-p) \geq 5.

records.content:
Because the Binomial takes integer values but the Normal is continuous, we adjust by \pm 0.5:

P(Y \leq k) \approx P\left(Z \leq \frac{k + 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right) — add 0.5 because the Normal must cover the full integer k

P(Y \geq k) \approx P\left(Z \geq \frac{k - 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right) — subtract 0.5

P(Y = k) \approx P\left(\frac{k - 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{npq}} \leq Z \leq \frac{k + 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{npq}}\right)

The continuity correction improves accuracy, especially when n is moderate (20–100).

EXAMPLE 5.18: Normal Approximation to the Binomial

The Problem.

A fair coin is flipped 100 times. Find the probability of getting at least 60 heads.

Solution.

Y \sim \text{Binomial}(100, 0.5). We have \mu = np = 50 and \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{25} = 5.

Check: np = 50 \geq 5 ✓ and n(1-p) = 50 \geq 5 ✓. The approximation is valid.

With continuity correction: P(Y \geq 60) \approx P\left(Z \geq \frac{59.5 - 50}{5}\right) = P(Z \geq 1.90) = 0.0287

Without continuity correction: P(Y \geq 60) \approx P\left(Z \geq \frac{60 - 50}{5}\right) = P(Z \geq 2.00) = 0.0228

Exact (Binomial): P(Y \geq 60) = \sum_{k=60}^{100}\binom{100}{k}(0.5)^{100} = 0.0284

The continuity-corrected answer (0.0287) is very close to the exact value (0.0284). The uncorrected version (0.0228) is noticeably off.

In R.# Exact Binomial
pbinom(59, 100, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)  # 0.02844

# Normal approximation WITH continuity correction
pnorm(59.5, 50, 5, lower.tail = FALSE)    # 0.02872

# Normal approximation WITHOUT continuity correction
pnorm(60, 50, 5, lower.tail = FALSE)      # 0.02275

Interpretation.

With 100 fair coin flips, there’s about a 2.8% chance of getting 60 or more heads. The Normal approximation with continuity correction nails this to within 0.03 percentage points. Without the correction, the error is about 0.6 percentage points — small but avoidable.

When n is large and both np \geq 5 and n(1-p) \geq 5, the Binomial(n, p) distribution is well approximated by N(np, np(1-p)). Exponential = Gamma(1, \beta) = Weibull(1, \beta)

Chi-Square(\nu) = Gamma(\nu/2, 2)

Uniform(0,1) = Beta(1, 1)

Poisson count ↔ Exponential gap (same process, different views)

🔬 What Did We Learn?

The distributions we’ve studied are not isolated — they form a connected family tree. The Exponential sits at the intersection of the Gamma and Weibull families. The Chi-Square bridges the Normal and Gamma worlds. The Uniform is a special case of the Beta. The Poisson process generates both Poisson counts and Exponential gaps.

Why this matters: When you encounter a new problem, you don’t pick a distribution at random. You reason from the physical process: “Events arrive at a constant rate → Poisson count → Exponential gap → Gamma for the kth event.” Or: “I’m modeling a proportion → Beta.” Or: “Wear-out failure → Weibull with \alpha > 1.” The family tree is your navigation chart.

Keep this reference table handy — you’ll use it throughout mathematical statistics and beyond.

records.content:
We now have all the tools to solve the problem from the chapter opening.

Setup: A needle of length \ell is dropped onto a floor with parallel lines spaced d apart (\ell \leq d). Two random variables describe the needle’s position:

\Theta = the acute angle between the needle and the lines, with \Theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \pi/2)

D = the distance from the needle’s center to the nearest line, with D \sim \text{Uniform}(0, d/2)

We assume \Theta and D are independent (the angle and position of a randomly dropped needle are unrelated).

When does the needle cross a line? The needle crosses if and only if the vertical projection of its half-length exceeds D:D \leq \frac{\ell}{2}\sin(\Theta)

The probability: Since \Theta and D are independent Uniforms, the joint density is constant over the rectangle [0, \pi/2] \times [0, d/2]. The probability of crossing is the ratio of the area where D \leq (\ell/2)\sin\theta to the total rectangle area:P(\text{cross}) = \frac{\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta \, d\theta}{\frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{d}{2}}

📐 Calculus Flashback: \int \sin\theta \, d\theta

\int \sin\theta \, d\theta = -\cos\theta + C, so \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\theta \, d\theta = [-\cos\theta]_0^{\pi/2} = -\cos(\pi/2) + \cos(0) = 0 + 1 = 1.P(\text{cross}) = \frac{(\ell/2) \cdot 1}{\pi d / 4} = \frac{\ell/2}{\pi d/4} = \frac{4\ell}{2\pi d} = \frac{2\ell}{\pi d}

And there it is — \pi emerges from the integral of \sin\theta over [0, \pi/2]. The circle was hiding in the rotation of the needle.# Buffon's Needle simulation
set.seed(42)
n_drops <- 100000
ell <- 1; d <- 2  # needle length 1, line spacing 2

theta <- runif(n_drops, 0, pi/2)
D <- runif(n_drops, 0, d/2)
crosses <- sum(D <= (ell/2) * sin(theta))

pi_estimate <- (2 * ell * n_drops) / (crosses * d)
cat("Estimated pi:", pi_estimate, "\n")
cat("Actual pi:   ", pi, "\n")
# Estimated pi: 3.143... (close!)

Chapter 5 Summary

Continuous random variables assign probability zero to every individual point. Probabilities exist only for intervals and are computed as areas under the probability density function via integration.

The PDF f(y) = F'(y) is the derivative of the CDF. It satisfies f(y) \geq 0 everywhere and \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y) \, dy = 1. The PDF is a density, not a probability — it can exceed 1.

Expected values for continuous RVs use integrals: E(Y) = \int y \, f(y) \, dy and V(Y) = E(Y^2) - \mu^2. The linearity rules E(aY+b) = a\mu + b and V(aY+b) = a^2\sigma^2 carry over unchanged from Chapter 4.

The Uniform distribution on (\theta_1, \theta_2) has constant density 1/(\theta_2 - \theta_1), mean (\theta_1 + \theta_2)/2, and variance (\theta_2 - \theta_1)^2/12. It is the engine of all random number generation.

The Normal distribution N(\mu, \sigma^2) is the bell curve. Standardize via Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma to use one table for all Normal distributions. The 68-95-99.7 rule gives quick probability estimates.

The Gamma distribution \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta) models right-skewed positive quantities. The Exponential (\alpha = 1) has the memoryless property and connects to the Poisson process. The Chi-Square (\alpha = \nu/2, \beta = 2) connects to squared standard Normals.

The Beta distribution \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) models proportions on [0, 1]. Its two parameters give it extraordinary shape flexibility.

Moment generating functions M(t) = E(e^{tY}) provide moments via derivatives (E(Y^k) = M^{(k)}(0)) and uniquely identify distributions.

Tchebysheff’s theorem guarantees at least 1 - 1/k^2 of probability within k standard deviations of the mean — for any distribution.

Buffon’s Needle connects continuous probability to geometry: the probability of a needle crossing a line involves the Uniform distribution, integration of \sin\theta, and \pi.

Think About It

You’ve now learned six named continuous distributions — Uniform, Normal, Gamma, Exponential, Chi-Square, Beta — each designed to model a different type of randomness. But here’s something to sit with: why are there so many?

The real world doesn’t come labeled “this is a Gamma distribution.” A data scientist looking at hospital wait times doesn’t see a mathematical formula — she sees a histogram. The act of choosing a distribution is a modeling decision: “I believe this data behaves approximately like a Gamma(3, 2).” The model is never the truth. It’s a useful approximation — and the utility depends on whether the approximation is close enough for the decision at hand.

So when you see a real dataset, how do you decide which distribution fits? That question — the bridge between theoretical distributions and messy data — is the central challenge of statistical inference, and it’s what the sequel to this book (Mathematical Statistics from the Ground Up) is all about.

5.R.3. Scores on a standardized test follow N(520, 10000).

(a) What proportion of scores are above 700? (b) What score separates the bottom 15% from the top 85%? (c) Two students take the test independently. What is the probability that both score above 600?

(c) How many drops would you need for an estimate accurate to 2 decimal places (in expectation)?

records.content:
Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Define and compute joint probability distributions (discrete and continuous)

Derive marginal distributions from joint distributions

Compute conditional distributions and conditional expectations

Determine whether random variables are independent

Calculate covariance and correlation between random variables

Find the expected value and variance of linear combinations of random variables

Prerequisites: Chapters 4–5. Builds on: PMFs, PDFs, CDFs, expected values, named distributions.

Content current as of April 2026.

The Opening Problem

Portfolio Risk. An investor holds two stocks. Stock A has an expected annual return of 12% with a standard deviation of 20%. Stock B has an expected return of 8% with a standard deviation of 15%. The investor puts 60% in A and 40% in B. What is the expected return and risk (standard deviation) of the portfolio?

If the stocks move independently, the answer is one number. If they tend to rise and fall together (positive correlation), the portfolio is riskier. If they move in opposite directions (negative correlation), the portfolio is safer — diversification works.

To answer this question precisely, we need to describe the joint behavior of two random variables simultaneously. That is what this chapter is about. Every concept from Chapters 4 and 5 — expected value, variance, distributions — generalizes from one variable to many.

records.content:
What Are We About to Learn?

Until now, every probability distribution we studied described a single random variable. But real-world problems almost always involve multiple random variables observed together. A medical study records both blood pressure and cholesterol. A manufacturer measures both length and diameter of each part. A portfolio tracks returns on multiple stocks simultaneously.

A joint distribution describes the probability behavior of two or more random variables considered together. It tells us not just about each variable individually, but about how they relate to each other.

records.content:
Definition: Joint Probability Density Function

If Y_1 and Y_2 are continuous random variables, their joint PDF f(y_1, y_2) satisfies:

f(y_1, y_2) \geq 0 for all (y_1, y_2)

\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_1\, dy_2 = 1

Probabilities are computed as double integrals:P((Y_1, Y_2) \in A) = \iint_A f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_1\, dy_2

📐 Calculus Flashback: Double Integrals

A double integral \int\int f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_1\, dy_2 is computed by iterated integration: integrate with respect to one variable while treating the other as a constant, then integrate the result.\int_a^b \int_c^d f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_a^b \left[\int_c^d f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_2\right] dy_1

The inner integral is done first (here, with respect to y_2), producing a function of y_1 alone, which is then integrated.

EXAMPLE: Joint Continuous Distribution. Let f(y_1, y_2) = 2(1 - y_1) for 0 \leq y_1 \leq 1, 0 \leq y_2 \leq 1.

Verification: \int_0^1\int_0^1 2(1-y_1)\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_0^1 2(1-y_1)[y_2]_0^1\, dy_1 = \int_0^1 2(1-y_1)\, dy_1 = [2y_1 - y_1^2]_0^1 = 2 - 1 = 1. \checkmark

Find P(Y_1 + Y_2 \leq 1):P(Y_1 + Y_2 \leq 1) = \int_0^1 \int_0^{1-y_1} 2(1-y_1)\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_0^1 2(1-y_1)^2\, dy_1 = \left[-\frac{2(1-y_1)^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{2}{3}

records.content:
The example above had a rectangular support: 0 \leq y_1 \leq 1, 0 \leq y_2 \leq 1. The limits of integration were constants, and life was easy. Most interesting joint distributions don’t have rectangular support. The region where f(y_1, y_2) > 0 is often a triangle, wedge, or other shape — and getting the integration limits right is the single most important skill in this chapter.

⚠️ The #1 Mistake in Multivariate Probability

When the support is NOT rectangular, the limits of the inner integral are functions of the outer variable, not constants. Students who blindly write \int_0^1 \int_0^1 when the support is a triangle will get every subsequent calculation wrong — marginals, conditionals, covariance, everything.

The fix: ALWAYS sketch the support region before writing any integral.

📐 Calculus Flashback: Setting Up Double Integral Limits

When the support region is not a rectangle, follow this procedure:

Step 1. Sketch the region in the (y_1, y_2)-plane. Shade it.

Step 2. Choose the order of integration. If integrating dy_2 first (inner) then dy_1 (outer):

Outer limits (for y_1): constants — the leftmost and rightmost extent of the region.

Inner limits (for y_2): functions of y_1 — for a fixed y_1, what are the lowest and highest y_2 values in the region?

Step 3. Write: \int_{y_1 = a}^{b} \int_{y_2 = g(y_1)}^{h(y_1)} f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_2\, dy_1

You can also integrate in the opposite order (dy_1 first). Sometimes one order is much easier than the other.

EXAMPLE M.1: Triangular Support — The Classic Case

The Problem.

Let f(y_1, y_2) = 6y_1 for 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 1, and f = 0 otherwise.

(a) Verify this is a valid PDF. (b) Find P(Y_2 < 0.5).

Solution.

The support region is the triangle where y_1 < y_2, both between 0 and 1. Sketch it: it’s the triangle above the line y_1 = y_2 in the unit square.

(a) Verify \int\int f = 1.

Integrate dy_2 first (inner). For a fixed y_1, y_2 ranges from y_1 to 1 (above the diagonal). Then y_1 ranges from 0 to 1:\int_0^1 \int_{y_1}^{1} 6y_1\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_0^1 6y_1(1 - y_1)\, dy_1 = \int_0^1 (6y_1 - 6y_1^2)\, dy_1= \left[3y_1^2 - 2y_1^3\right]_0^1 = 3 - 2 = 1 \quad \checkmark

(b) P(Y_2 < 0.5): the region is 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 0.5.P(Y_2 < 0.5) = \int_0^{0.5} \int_{y_1}^{0.5} 6y_1\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_0^{0.5} 6y_1(0.5 - y_1)\, dy_1 = \int_0^{0.5}(3y_1 - 6y_1^2)\, dy_1= \left[\frac{3y_1^2}{2} - 2y_1^3\right]_0^{0.5} = \frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8} = 0.125

EXAMPLE M.2: Finding the Constant c

The Problem.

Find the constant c that makes f(y_1, y_2) = c(y_1 + y_2) a valid joint PDF on the triangular region 0 \leq y_1 \leq 1, 0 \leq y_2 \leq 1 - y_1.

Solution.

The support is the triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (0,1). For a fixed y_1, y_2 ranges from 0 to 1 - y_1.

Set \int\int f = 1:c\int_0^1 \int_0^{1-y_1} (y_1 + y_2)\, dy_2\, dy_1 = 1

Inner integral (treat y_1 as constant):\int_0^{1-y_1}(y_1 + y_2)\, dy_2 = \left[y_1 y_2 + \frac{y_2^2}{2}\right]_0^{1-y_1} = y_1(1-y_1) + \frac{(1-y_1)^2}{2}= (1-y_1)\left[y_1 + \frac{1-y_1}{2}\right] = (1-y_1) \cdot \frac{1+y_1}{2} = \frac{1-y_1^2}{2}

Outer integral:c \int_0^1 \frac{1-y_1^2}{2}\, dy_1 = \frac{c}{2}\left[y_1 - \frac{y_1^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{c}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{c}{3} = 1

Therefore c = 3.

EXAMPLE M.3: Infinite Wedge Support (Exponential-Type)

The Problem.

The total time at a service window is Y_1 and the waiting time in line is Y_2, with joint density f(y_1, y_2) = e^{-y_1} for 0 \leq y_2 \leq y_1 < \infty.

(a) Verify this is a valid PDF. (b) Find P(Y_1 > 2).

Solution.

The support is the infinite wedge below the line y_2 = y_1 in the first quadrant. Since y_2 \leq y_1, for a fixed y_1, y_2 ranges from 0 to y_1.

(a) \int_0^{\infty}\int_0^{y_1} e^{-y_1}\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_0^{\infty} y_1 e^{-y_1}\, dy_1

This is E(Y) for Y \sim \text{Exponential}(1), which equals 1. \checkmark

(Or by integration by parts: \int_0^{\infty} y_1 e^{-y_1}\, dy_1 = [-y_1 e^{-y_1}]_0^{\infty} + \int_0^{\infty} e^{-y_1}\, dy_1 = 0 + 1 = 1.)

(b) P(Y_1 > 2) = \int_2^{\infty}\int_0^{y_1} e^{-y_1}\, dy_2\, dy_1 = \int_2^{\infty} y_1 e^{-y_1}\, dy_1

By integration by parts: = [-y_1 e^{-y_1}]_2^{\infty} + \int_2^{\infty} e^{-y_1}\, dy_1 = 2e^{-2} + e^{-2} = 3e^{-2} \approx 0.4060.

EXAMPLE M.4: Choosing the Integration Order

The Problem.

Let f(y_1, y_2) = 24y_1 y_2 for 0 < y_1 < 1, 0 < y_2 < 1, y_1 + y_2 < 1. Find P(Y_1 > Y_2).

Solution.

The support is the triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) — the same region as Example M.2. The additional constraint for this probability is y_1 > y_2.

The region where y_1 > y_2 AND y_1 + y_2 < 1 is the triangle below y_2 = y_1 and below y_2 = 1 - y_1.

Order 1: dy_2 first. For fixed y_1, y_2 ranges from 0 to \min(y_1, 1-y_1). When y_1 < 0.5: upper limit is y_1. When y_1 \geq 0.5: upper limit is 1 - y_1. This requires splitting into two integrals — messy.

Order 2: dy_1 first. For fixed y_2, y_1 ranges from y_2 (since y_1 > y_2) to 1 - y_2 (since y_1 + y_2 < 1). Then y_2 ranges from 0 to 0.5 (at y_2 = 0.5, y_1 = y_2 meets y_1 + y_2 = 1). One integral — much cleaner.P(Y_1 > Y_2) = \int_0^{0.5}\int_{y_2}^{1-y_2} 24y_1 y_2\, dy_1\, dy_2

Inner: \int_{y_2}^{1-y_2} 24y_1 y_2\, dy_1 = 24y_2 \cdot \frac{y_1^2}{2}\Big|_{y_2}^{1-y_2} = 12y_2[(1-y_2)^2 - y_2^2] = 12y_2(1-2y_2)

Outer: \int_0^{0.5} 12y_2(1-2y_2)\, dy_2 = 12\int_0^{0.5}(y_2 - 2y_2^2)\, dy_2 = 12\left[\frac{y_2^2}{2} - \frac{2y_2^3}{3}\right]_0^{0.5}= 12\left[\frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{12}\right] = 12 \cdot \frac{1}{24} = \frac{1}{2}

By symmetry of 24y_1 y_2 in y_1 and y_2 on this symmetric region, P(Y_1 > Y_2) = 1/2 makes perfect sense.

records.content:
What Are We About to Learn?

Given the joint distribution of (Y_1, Y_2), we often want the distribution of Y_1 alone — ignoring Y_2. This is the marginal distribution. It’s obtained by “summing out” (discrete) or “integrating out” (continuous) the other variable.

The critical warning: When the support is not rectangular, the limits of integration for the marginal depend on the variable you’re keeping. This is where most errors occur.

Definition: Marginal Distributions

Discrete: p_1(y_1) = \sum_{y_2} p(y_1, y_2) and p_2(y_2) = \sum_{y_1} p(y_1, y_2)

Continuous: f_1(y_1) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_2 and f_2(y_2) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(y_1, y_2)\, dy_1

Key point for non-rectangular support: The “-\infty to \infty” limits really mean “over all y_2 values where f(y_1, y_2) > 0 for this particular y_1.” When the support is a triangle, these limits are functions of y_1.

EXAMPLE (Discrete marginals). From the smartphone table, the marginal of Y_1 (screen defects) is:p_1(0) = 0.80 + 0.05 = 0.85, \quad p_1(1) = 0.10 + 0.05 = 0.15

This is the row totals column — the distribution of screen defects ignoring battery status.

EXAMPLE (Rectangular support). For f(y_1, y_2) = 2(1-y_1) on [0,1]^2:f_1(y_1) = \int_0^1 2(1-y_1)\, dy_2 = 2(1-y_1), \quad 0 \leq y_1 \leq 1f_2(y_2) = \int_0^1 2(1-y_1)\, dy_1 = [2y_1 - y_1^2]_0^1 = 1, \quad 0 \leq y_2 \leq 1

So Y_2 \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1) but Y_1 has the triangular density 2(1-y_1).

EXAMPLE M.5: Marginals from a Triangular Support

The Problem.

From Example M.1: f(y_1, y_2) = 6y_1 for 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 1. Find f_1(y_1) and f_2(y_2).

Solution.

Finding f_1(y_1): Integrate out y_2. For a fixed y_1, y_2 ranges from y_1 to 1 (the support constraint y_1 < y_2 < 1):f_1(y_1) = \int_{y_1}^{1} 6y_1\, dy_2 = 6y_1(1 - y_1), \quad 0 < y_1 < 1

Common error: Writing \int_0^1 6y_1\, dy_2 = 6y_1 — WRONG! The lower limit is y_1, not 0, because y_2 > y_1 in this support.

Finding f_2(y_2): Integrate out y_1. For a fixed y_2, y_1 ranges from 0 to y_2 (the constraint 0 < y_1 < y_2):f_2(y_2) = \int_0^{y_2} 6y_1\, dy_1 = 6 \cdot \frac{y_1^2}{2}\Big|_0^{y_2} = 3y_2^2, \quad 0 < y_2 < 1

Verification: \int_0^1 6y_1(1-y_1)\, dy_1 = [3y_1^2 - 2y_1^3]_0^1 = 1 \checkmark and \int_0^1 3y_2^2\, dy_2 = [y_2^3]_0^1 = 1 \checkmark.

EXAMPLE M.6: Marginals from the Infinite Wedge

The Problem.

From Example M.3: f(y_1, y_2) = e^{-y_1} for 0 \leq y_2 \leq y_1 < \infty. Find both marginals.

Solution.

f_1(y_1): Integrate out y_2 from 0 to y_1:f_1(y_1) = \int_0^{y_1} e^{-y_1}\, dy_2 = y_1 e^{-y_1}, \quad y_1 > 0

This is a \text{Gamma}(2, 1) distribution. Check: \int_0^{\infty} y_1 e^{-y_1}\, dy_1 = 1 \checkmark.

f_2(y_2): Integrate out y_1 from y_2 to \infty (since y_1 \geq y_2):f_2(y_2) = \int_{y_2}^{\infty} e^{-y_1}\, dy_1 = e^{-y_2}, \quad y_2 \geq 0

This is an \text{Exponential}(1) distribution. Check: \int_0^{\infty} e^{-y_2}\, dy_2 = 1 \checkmark.

Interpretation: The total service time (Y_1) follows a Gamma(2,1), while the waiting time (Y_2) follows an Exponential(1).

records.content:
What Are We About to Learn?

In Chapter 3, we defined P(A|B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B). The same idea extends to random variables: the conditional distribution of Y_1 given Y_2 = y_2 describes Y_1’s behavior when we know the value of Y_2.

Why this is hard: For non-rectangular support, the range of Y_1 changes depending on the value of Y_2. When f(y_1, y_2) = 6y_1 on 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 1, the conditional distribution of Y_1 given Y_2 = 0.8 has support (0, 0.8), but given Y_2 = 0.3 it has support (0, 0.3).

Definition: Conditional Distribution

Discrete: p(y_1 | y_2) = \frac{p(y_1, y_2)}{p_2(y_2)}, provided p_2(y_2) > 0.

Continuous: f(y_1 | y_2) = \frac{f(y_1, y_2)}{f_2(y_2)}, provided f_2(y_2) > 0.

EXAMPLE (Discrete). From the smartphone data: P(Y_1 = 1 | Y_2 = 1) = \frac{p(1,1)}{p_2(1)} = \frac{0.05}{0.10} = 0.50.

Among phones with battery defects, 50% also have screen defects — much higher than the unconditional rate of 15%. The two defect types are associated.

EXAMPLE M.7: Conditional Distribution — Triangular Support

The Problem.

For f(y_1, y_2) = 6y_1 on 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 1 (Example M.1), find f(y_1 | y_2) and compute E(Y_1 | Y_2 = 0.8).

Solution.

From Example M.5, f_2(y_2) = 3y_2^2.f(y_1 | y_2) = \frac{f(y_1, y_2)}{f_2(y_2)} = \frac{6y_1}{3y_2^2} = \frac{2y_1}{y_2^2}, \quad 0 < y_1 < y_2

Verify it’s a valid density:\int_0^{y_2} \frac{2y_1}{y_2^2}\, dy_1 = \frac{2}{y_2^2} \cdot \frac{y_1^2}{2}\Big|_0^{y_2} = \frac{y_2^2}{y_2^2} = 1 \quad \checkmark

Conditional expectation:E(Y_1 | Y_2 = y_2) = \int_0^{y_2} y_1 \cdot \frac{2y_1}{y_2^2}\, dy_1 = \frac{2}{y_2^2}\int_0^{y_2} y_1^2\, dy_1 = \frac{2}{y_2^2} \cdot \frac{y_2^3}{3} = \frac{2y_2}{3}

At y_2 = 0.8: E(Y_1 | Y_2 = 0.8) = \frac{2(0.8)}{3} = \frac{1.6}{3} \approx 0.533.

Notice: E(Y_1 | Y_2 = y_2) = \frac{2y_2}{3} is a function of y_2, not a single number. The larger Y_2 is, the larger Y_1 tends to be — which makes sense because Y_1 < Y_2.

EXAMPLE M.8: Verifying the Tower Property

The Problem.

Using Example M.7, verify that E[E(Y_1 | Y_2)] = E(Y_1).

Solution.

We found E(Y_1 | Y_2 = y_2) = \frac{2y_2}{3}, so E(Y_1 | Y_2) = \frac{2Y_2}{3} as a random variable.E\left[\frac{2Y_2}{3}\right] = \frac{2}{3} E(Y_2) = \frac{2}{3}\int_0^1 y_2 \cdot 3y_2^2\, dy_2 = \frac{2}{3}\int_0^1 3y_2^3\, dy_2 = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{2}

Check directly: E(Y_1) = \int_0^1 y_1 \cdot 6y_1(1-y_1)\, dy_1 = \int_0^1 (6y_1^2 - 6y_1^3)\, dy_1 = 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \quad \checkmark

The Tower Property holds: E[E(Y_1|Y_2)] = E(Y_1) = 1/2.

records.content:
What Are We About to Learn?

Two random variables are independent if knowing the value of one tells you nothing about the other. Mathematically, their joint distribution factors into the product of marginals.

A powerful shortcut: If the support region is not rectangular, the variables are automatically dependent — no calculation needed. Independence requires both that the support is rectangular AND that f factors.

Definition: Independence

Y_1 and Y_2 are independent if and only if:f(y_1, y_2) = f_1(y_1) \cdot f_2(y_2) \quad \text{for all } (y_1, y_2)

(Use p for discrete, f for continuous.)

The Rectangular Support Shortcut

Quick test for dependence: If the support region of f(y_1, y_2) is NOT rectangular (e.g., triangular, wedge, circular), then Y_1 and Y_2 are automatically dependent — no calculation needed.

Why? If the support is 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 1, knowing Y_2 = 0.3 restricts Y_1 to (0, 0.3). That’s information — so they can’t be independent.

Quick test for independence: If the support IS rectangular AND f(y_1, y_2) = g(y_1) \cdot h(y_2) (the density factors into a function of y_1 alone times a function of y_2 alone), then Y_1 and Y_2 are independent.

Checking the smartphone example: p(0,0) = 0.80 but p_1(0) \cdot p_2(0) = 0.85 \times 0.90 = 0.765 \neq 0.80. Not independent. The defects are associated.

Checking f(y_1,y_2) = 2(1-y_1) on [0,1]^2: Support is rectangular ✓. Does f factor? f = 2(1-y_1) \cdot 1 = g(y_1) \cdot h(y_2) ✓. Independent!

Checking f(y_1,y_2) = 6y_1 on 0 < y_1 < y_2 < 1: Support is triangular (NOT rectangular). Dependent — no calculation needed! We confirmed this: E(Y_1|Y_2 = y_2) = 2y_2/3, which depends on y_2.

Theorem: Independence and Expectations

If Y_1 and Y_2 are independent, then for any functions g_1 and g_2:E[g_1(Y_1) \cdot g_2(Y_2)] = E[g_1(Y_1)] \cdot E[g_2(Y_2)]

Proof. E[g_1(Y_1)g_2(Y_2)] = \int\int g_1(y_1)g_2(y_2)f(y_1,y_2)\,dy_1\,dy_2. Since f = f_1 \cdot f_2 by independence:= \int\int g_1(y_1)g_2(y_2)f_1(y_1)f_2(y_2)\,dy_1\,dy_2 = \left[\int g_1(y_1)f_1(y_1)\,dy_1\right]\left[\int g_2(y_2)f_2(y_2)\,dy_2\right]= E[g_1(Y_1)] \cdot E[g_2(Y_2)]. \quad \blacksquare

The factoring step works because g_1(y_1)f_1(y_1) does not depend on y_2, so it factors out of the dy_2 integral.
