Theorem 7.7: Joint PDF of All Order Statistics

Let Y_1, \ldots, Y_n be iid with PDF f(y). The joint PDF of the order statistics (Y_{(1)}, Y_{(2)}, \ldots, Y_{(n)}) is:f_{Y_{(1)}, \ldots, Y_{(n)}}(y_1, \ldots, y_n) = n! \prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i), \quad y_1 < y_2 < \cdots < y_n

and zero otherwise.

PROOF

Strategy: The joint PDF of the original (unsorted) sample (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n) is \prod f(y_i) by independence. The order statistics are a specific sorted arrangement. We count how many original orderings produce the same sorted result.

Step 1: The joint PDF of the original iid sample is:f_{Y_1, \ldots, Y_n}(y_1, \ldots, y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i)

Step 2: Consider a specific sorted sequence y_1 < y_2 < \cdots < y_n. How many orderings of the original sample produce this exact sorted sequence as the order statistics? The answer is n! — any of the n! permutations of the indices maps to the same sorted order. (For example, if n = 3 and the sorted values are 0.2 < 0.5 < 0.9, then (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3) could be any of the 6 permutations (0.2, 0.5, 0.9), (0.2, 0.9, 0.5), (0.5, 0.2, 0.9), etc., and all six produce the same order statistics (Y_{(1)}, Y_{(2)}, Y_{(3)}) = (0.2, 0.5, 0.9).)

Step 3: Since each of these n! permutations contributes probability density \prod f(y_i) to the sorted sequence, and they are mutually exclusive (continuous random variables have probability 0 of ties), the total density at the sorted point is:f_{Y_{(1)}, \ldots, Y_{(n)}}(y_1, \ldots, y_n) = n! \prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i), \quad y_1 < y_2 < \cdots < y_n

The restriction y_1 < y_2 < \cdots < y_n is essential: order statistics are defined to be sorted, so the density is zero outside this region.

∎

The factor n! accounts for the n! ways the original random sample could have produced this sorted order. This result is the foundation for deriving the joint distribution of any subset of order statistics (e.g., the joint distribution of Y_{(1)} and Y_{(n)} used in range problems).

Guided Practice 7.6

A system has 5 identical components with independent lifetimes Y_i \sim \text{Exponential}(\beta = 100) hours. The system fails when the first component fails. Find the distribution of the system lifetime and its expected value.

Click for Solution

System lifetime = Y_{(1)} = \min(Y_1, \ldots, Y_5).

For Exponential(\beta = 100): f(y) = \frac{1}{100}e^{-y/100}, F(y) = 1 - e^{-y/100}.f_{Y_{(1)}}(y) = 5[1 - F(y)]^4 f(y) = 5[e^{-y/100}]^4 \cdot \frac{1}{100}e^{-y/100} = \frac{5}{100}e^{-5y/100} = \frac{1}{20}e^{-y/20}

This is \text{Exponential}(\beta = 20). So E(Y_{(1)}) = 20 hours.

The expected system lifetime is 5 times shorter than each component’s expected lifetime. This is a fundamental result in reliability engineering: redundancy helps, but the weakest link sets the pace.

📌 What Did We Learn?

Order statistics answer questions about extremes and rankings in random samples. The maximum Y_{(n)} has CDF [F(y)]^n — the probability that the maximum is below y equals the probability that ALL observations are below y. The minimum Y_{(1)} has survival function [1-F(y)]^n. The general kth order statistic has a combinatorial formula that counts the ways to place observations above, at, and below the value y. In practice, order statistics model the strongest wave (coastal engineering), the first failure (reliability), the fastest runner (sports), and the median observation (robust statistics). For Exponential lifetimes, the minimum of n independent Exp(\beta) is Exp(\beta/n) — redundancy shortens expected system lifetime linearly.

records.content:
🎯 What Are We Going to Learn?

This section is enrichment material. Your instructor may skip it if time is limited, but the ideas here are used throughout simulation, statistics, and data science.

We prove a beautiful result: if X is any continuous random variable with CDF F, then F(X) \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1). This is the Probability Integral Transform (PIT). Its reverse — the Inverse CDF Method — lets us generate random samples from any distribution using only Uniform(0, 1) random numbers. This is how every statistical software package simulates random variables.

Theorem 7.8: The Probability Integral Transform

Let X be a continuous random variable with strictly increasing CDF F_X. Define U = F_X(X). Then U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1).

PROOF

Strategy: Apply the CDF method. Since F_X is a CDF, it maps from (-\infty, \infty) to (0, 1), so U takes values in (0, 1). We compute F_U(u) directly.

Step 1: Since F_X is strictly increasing, it has an inverse F_X^{-1}. So:F_U(u) = P(U \leq u) = P(F_X(X) \leq u) = P(X \leq F_X^{-1}(u))

(Why? Because F_X is increasing, F_X(X) \leq u if and only if X \leq F_X^{-1}(u).)

Step 2: By the definition of CDF:P(X \leq F_X^{-1}(u)) = F_X(F_X^{-1}(u)) = u

Step 3: So F_U(u) = u for 0 < u < 1, which is the CDF of Uniform(0, 1).

∎

WHY THIS MATTERS: The PIT says that every continuous distribution, when passed through its own CDF, becomes Uniform(0, 1). This is remarkable — it means that behind every distribution lurks a uniform random variable. Running the process in reverse gives us a simulation method:

The Inverse CDF Method (for simulation)

To generate a random value X from any continuous distribution with CDF F_X:

Step 1: Generate U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1) (every programming language can do this).

Step 2: Compute X = F_X^{-1}(U).

Then X has the desired distribution.

EXAMPLE 7.19: Generating Exponential Random Variables

The Problem.

Use the inverse CDF method to generate random values from an \text{Exponential}(\beta) distribution.

Solution.

The CDF of \text{Exponential}(\beta) is F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\beta} for x > 0.

Step 1: Set u = F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\beta} and solve for x:u = 1 - e^{-x/\beta} \implies e^{-x/\beta} = 1 - u \implies -x/\beta = \ln(1 - u) \implies x = -\beta\ln(1 - u)

(Calculus flashback: to solve e^{-x/\beta} = 1 - u, take \ln of both sides: -x/\beta = \ln(1-u), then multiply by -\beta.)

Step 2: Since U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1) implies 1 - U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1) (by symmetry), we can simplify to X = -\beta \ln(U).

So: generate U \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1), then X = -\beta \ln(U) gives X \sim \text{Exponential}(\beta).

In R.# Generate 10000 Exponential(3) values using inverse CDF method
set.seed(42)
beta <- 3
u <- runif(10000)
x_manual <- -beta * log(u)       # Our method
x_builtin <- rexp(10000, rate = 1/beta)  # R's built-in

# Compare
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(x_manual, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, main = "Inverse CDF Method",
     col = "steelblue", border = "white", xlab = "x")
curve(dexp(x, rate = 1/beta), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

hist(x_builtin, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, main = "R's rexp()",
     col = "steelblue", border = "white", xlab = "x")
curve(dexp(x, rate = 1/beta), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

Both histograms match the theoretical Exponential PDF — our hand-built method is identical to what R does internally.

📌 What Did We Learn?

The Probability Integral Transform is one of the most elegant results in probability: passing any continuous random variable through its own CDF yields a Uniform(0, 1). Running this in reverse — the Inverse CDF Method — is how computers generate random variables from any distribution. Every call to rexp(), rnorm(), rgamma() in R ultimately relies on this idea (sometimes with additional tricks for efficiency). This connects the abstract theory of Chapter 7 to the practical simulations you’ve been running since Chapter 1.

records.content:
🎯 What Are We Going to Learn?

This section ties together the PIT (Section 7.7), the multivariable Jacobian (Section 7.5), and polar coordinates into one of the most elegant results in computational statistics.

The Inverse CDF Method generates random variables from any distribution — if you can invert the CDF. But the Normal distribution has no closed-form CDF inverse. So how does your computer generate rnorm() values? The Box-Muller Transform (1958): generate two independent N(0,1) from two independent \text{Unif}(0,1).

Theorem 7.9: The Box-Muller Transform

Let U_1, U_2 be independent \text{Uniform}(0, 1). Define:Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\;\cos(2\pi U_2), \qquad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\;\sin(2\pi U_2)

Then Z_1 and Z_2 are independent N(0, 1) random variables.

PROOF

Strategy: Work backwards. Start with two independent N(0,1) variables, convert to polar coordinates using a Jacobian, and show the polar components are functions of Uniform random variables.

Step 1: Joint density of two independent standard normals.

If Z_1, Z_2 \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1), their joint PDF is:f_{Z_1, Z_2}(z_1, z_2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z_1^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z_2^2/2} = \frac{1}{2\pi} e^{-(z_1^2 + z_2^2)/2}

Notice: this depends on z_1 and z_2 only through z_1^2 + z_2^2 = r^2 — it’s rotationally symmetric. This is the key insight.

Step 2: Convert to polar coordinates.

Define R \geq 0 and 0 \leq \Theta < 2\pi by Z_1 = R\cos\Theta, Z_2 = R\sin\Theta.

(Calculus flashback: The Jacobian of polar-to-Cartesian is |J| = r. This comes from the area element dA = r\,dr\,d\theta. Specifically: \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial r} = \cos\theta, \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial \theta} = -r\sin\theta, \frac{\partial z_2}{\partial r} = \sin\theta, \frac{\partial z_2}{\partial \theta} = r\cos\theta. Determinant: r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r.)

Applying Theorem 7.3 with |J| = r:f_{R, \Theta}(r, \theta) = \frac{1}{2\pi} e^{-r^2/2} \cdot r

for r > 0, 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.

Step 3: Factor into independent components.f_{R, \Theta}(r, \theta) = \underbrace{r \, e^{-r^2/2}}_{\text{PDF of } R \text{ (Rayleigh)}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{2\pi}}_{\text{PDF of } \Theta \text{ (Uniform)}}

The joint PDF factors as g(r) \cdot h(\theta), so R and \Theta are independent. \Theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 2\pi) and R has the Rayleigh PDF f_R(r) = re^{-r^2/2}.

Step 4: Express R and \Theta via Uniforms using the Inverse CDF Method.

For \Theta: Since \Theta \sim \text{Unif}(0, 2\pi), set \Theta = 2\pi U_2 where U_2 \sim \text{Unif}(0,1).

For R: The CDF is F_R(r) = \int_0^r t\,e^{-t^2/2}\,dt. Using u-substitution with w = t^2/2, dw = t\,dt:F_R(r) = \int_0^{r^2/2} e^{-w}\,dw = 1 - e^{-r^2/2}

Set U_1 = F_R(R) = 1 - e^{-R^2/2} and solve for R:e^{-R^2/2} = 1 - U_1 \implies R^2/2 = -\ln(1 - U_1) \implies R = \sqrt{-2\ln(1 - U_1)}

Since 1 - U_1 \sim \text{Unif}(0,1) when U_1 \sim \text{Unif}(0,1), we simplify: R = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}.

Step 5: Substitute back into Z_1 = R\cos\Theta, Z_2 = R\sin\Theta:Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\;\cos(2\pi U_2), \qquad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\;\sin(2\pi U_2)

∎

WHY THIS IS BEAUTIFUL: One result that uses every major idea from this chapter — the Jacobian (polar coordinates), the PIT (generating R from U_1), independence via factorization (Step 3), and the rotational symmetry of the Normal distribution. This is how GPU-based scientific computing generates billions of normal random numbers.# Box-Muller in action
set.seed(42)
n <- 10000
u1 <- runif(n); u2 <- runif(n)
z1 <- sqrt(-2 * log(u1)) * cos(2 * pi * u2)
z2 <- sqrt(-2 * log(u1)) * sin(2 * pi * u2)
cat("Z1: mean =", round(mean(z1), 3), " sd =", round(sd(z1), 3), "\n")
cat("Z2: mean =", round(mean(z2), 3), " sd =", round(sd(z2), 3), "\n")
cat("Cor(Z1,Z2) =", round(cor(z1, z2), 4), "\n")

⚠️ Common Mistakes — Chapter 7 Summary

CDF Method: Forgetting to flip the inequality for decreasing transformations. P(g(X) \leq u) = P(X \geq g^{-1}(u)) when g is decreasing.

Transformation Method: Forgetting the absolute value. The formula is f_U(u) = f_X(h^{-1}(u)) \cdot |dh^{-1}/du|. Without the absolute value, you can get a negative PDF.

MGF Method: Applying it to sums with different scale parameters. The Gamma summation result requires the same \beta. You cannot directly add \text{Gamma}(\alpha_1, \beta_1) and \text{Gamma}(\alpha_2, \beta_2) when \beta_1 \neq \beta_2 — the result is not Gamma.

Jacobian: Computing the wrong determinant. The Jacobian matrix has \partial x_i / \partial u_j, not \partial u_i / \partial x_j. If you compute the “forward” Jacobian (\partial u / \partial x) instead of the “inverse” Jacobian (\partial x / \partial u), you get 1/|J| instead of |J|.

Order Statistics: Confusing F(y) and f(y). The order statistic formulas use both the CDF and the PDF. Students who plug in f(y) where F(y) should go (or vice versa) get the wrong answer.

Chapter 7 Summary

The central question of this chapter: if X has a known distribution and U = g(X), what is the distribution of U? Three methods answer this question.

The CDF Method is universal: compute F_U(u) = P(U \leq u) by substituting g(X) for U, solve for X, and differentiate. It works for any transformation, including non-one-to-one functions like X^2.

The Transformation Method gives a direct formula for one-to-one functions: f_U(u) = f_X(h^{-1}(u)) \cdot |dh^{-1}/du|. The absolute derivative acts as a “probability density stretching factor.”

The MGF Method exploits the fact that MGFs of sums of independent variables multiply: M_U(t) = \prod M_{X_i}(t). If the product matches a known MGF, the distribution is identified. Key closure results: Normal + Normal = Normal; Gamma + Gamma (same \beta) = Gamma; Binomial + Binomial (same p) = Binomial; Poisson + Poisson = Poisson.

Multivariable transformations use a Jacobian determinant: f_{U_1, U_2}(u_1, u_2) = f_{X_1, X_2}(g_1, g_2) \cdot |J|, where J is the determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of the inverse transformation.

Order statistics — the sorted values Y_{(1)} \leq Y_{(2)} \leq \cdots \leq Y_{(n)} — have explicit PDFs. The maximum has CDF [F(y)]^n. The minimum has survival function [1-F(y)]^n. The kth order statistic has PDF involving binomial coefficients.

The Gamma-to-Beta transformation (Example 7.15) is arguably the most important result in this chapter: if Y_1 \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_1, 1) and Y_2 \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_2, 1) are independent, then Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2) \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_1, \alpha_2) and is independent of Y_1 + Y_2 \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2, 1).

Everything in mathematical statistics depends on this chapter. Sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, ANOVA — they all require finding the distribution of functions of random variables. You now have the tools.

Think About It

💭 Tell Your Brain

You’ve just learned three methods for finding the distribution of a transformed random variable. Here’s the deep question: why do we need three methods instead of just one?

The CDF method always works — so why bother with the others? Because mathematics rewards having multiple perspectives on the same problem. The transformation method reveals that probability density stretches and compresses like a physical material. The MGF method reveals that adding independent random variables corresponds to multiplying their characteristic functions — a duality between addition and multiplication that runs through all of mathematics.

The real lesson isn’t the formulas. It’s this: knowing the distribution of an input is not the same as knowing the distribution of an output. Every model, every formula, every algorithm transforms data. And every transformation changes the distribution. The next time someone tells you “the data is normally distributed,” ask: “the raw data, or the data after your transformation?” The answer matters. That’s what this chapter taught you to see.

🌟 Going Deeper: When You Don’t Need the Exact Distribution

Sometimes you do not need the exact distribution of U = g(Y) — you just need a good approximation of its mean and variance. The Delta Method provides exactly this, using nothing more than a first-order Taylor series approximation. It is one of the most frequently used tools in mathematical statistics and applied work.

This section previews material from Mathematical Statistics (MATH 4200). You can skip it without losing continuity, but it will give you a head start when you encounter it next semester.

records.content:
If Y is a random variable with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, and g is a differentiable function, then we can approximate g(Y) near \mu using a Taylor expansion:g(Y) \approx g(\mu) + g'(\mu)(Y - \mu)

This is a linear approximation. Taking the expectation of both sides:E[g(Y)] \approx g(\mu) + g'(\mu) \cdot \underbrace{E[Y - \mu]}_{= 0} = g(\mu)

Taking the variance:\text{Var}(g(Y)) \approx [g'(\mu)]^2 \cdot \text{Var}(Y) = [g'(\mu)]^2 \sigma^2

🔑 The Delta Method

If Y has mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, and g is differentiable with g'(\mu) \ne 0, then:E[g(Y)] \approx g(\mu), \qquad \text{Var}(g(Y)) \approx [g'(\mu)]^2 \sigma^2

In words: The mean of the transformed variable is approximately the function applied to the mean. The variance of the transformed variable is the original variance multiplied by the square of the derivative evaluated at the mean.

records.content:
Example D.1 (Variance of a Reciprocal). Suppose Y has mean \mu = 10 and variance \sigma^2 = 4. You need the variance of U = 1/Y.

Here g(y) = 1/y and g'(y) = -1/y^2, so g'(\mu) = -1/100.\text{Var}(1/Y) \approx \left(-\frac{1}{100}\right)^2 \cdot 4 = \frac{4}{10{,}000} = 0.0004

No transformation theorem needed — just one line of calculus.

Example D.2 (Variance of a Log-Return). Stock returns are often analyzed as U = \ln(Y) where Y is the gross return. If Y has mean \mu = 1.08 and \sigma^2 = 0.04:

g(y) = \ln(y), g'(y) = 1/y, g'(\mu) = 1/1.08 \approx 0.926.\text{Var}(\ln Y) \approx (0.926)^2 \cdot 0.04 = 0.0343

Compare with the exact answer (if Y were lognormal): \ln(1 + 0.04/1.08^2) = \ln(1.0343) = 0.0337. The approximation is very close!

Example D.3 (Variance Stabilizing Transformation for Poisson). If X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) with large \lambda, then E[X] = \lambda and \text{Var}(X) = \lambda. The variance depends on the mean, which is inconvenient for many statistical procedures.

Let U = \sqrt{X}. By the Delta Method with g(x) = \sqrt{x} and g'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}:\text{Var}(\sqrt{X}) \approx \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)^2 \cdot \lambda = \frac{\lambda}{4\lambda} = \frac{1}{4}

The variance of \sqrt{X} is approximately 1/4, regardless of \lambda! This is why the square root transformation is used to “stabilize” the variance of Poisson data — a result you will use extensively in regression analysis and ANOVA.

✅ What Did We Learn?

The Delta Method approximates E[g(Y)] \approx g(\mu) and \text{Var}(g(Y)) \approx [g'(\mu)]^2 \sigma^2 using a first-order Taylor expansion.

When to use it: When you need the mean and variance of a transformation but finding the exact distribution is too difficult or unnecessary.

Key applications:

Approximating standard errors of transformed estimators (confidence intervals in the next course)

Variance stabilizing transformations (\sqrt{X} for Poisson, \arcsin\sqrt{p} for proportions)

Quick approximations in applied work when an exact answer is overkill

Connection to this chapter: The Delta Method and the transformation method answer related but different questions. The transformation method finds the exact distribution. The Delta Method finds approximate mean and variance. When the exact distribution is available, use it. When it is not, the Delta Method is your best friend.

🖥️ Putting It All Together in R

Throughout this chapter, we derived densities by hand using four methods. In this mini-lab, we bring all four methods together in one comprehensive simulation that verifies every major result of the chapter. Run this code and watch the math come alive.
# ================================================================
# CHAPTER 6 GRAND VERIFICATION: Functions of Random Variables
# ================================================================

set.seed(2026)
n <- 200000  # simulation size

cat("========================================\n")
cat("  CHAPTER 6: ALL METHODS VERIFIED IN R  \n")
cat("========================================\n\n")

# ------ METHOD 1: CDF Method (Max of two uniforms) ------
Y1 <- runif(n); Y2 <- runif(n)
U_max <- pmax(Y1, Y2)
cat("CDF Method — Max of 2 Uniform(0,1):\n")
cat("  Theoretical E[max] = 2/3 =", round(2/3, 4), "\n")
cat("  Simulated E[max]   =", round(mean(U_max), 4), "\n\n")

# ------ METHOD 2: Transformation (Lognormal) ------
X <- rnorm(n, mean = 1, sd = 0.5)
S <- exp(X)
cat("Transformation — exp(N(1, 0.25)) = Lognormal:\n")
cat("  Theoretical mean = exp(mu + sigma^2/2) =", round(exp(1 + 0.25/2), 4), "\n")
cat("  Simulated mean   =", round(mean(S), 4), "\n\n")

# ------ METHOD 3: MGF (Sum of independent normals) ------
Y_sum <- rnorm(n, 3, 1) + rnorm(n, -1, 2) + rnorm(n, 5, 0.5)
cat("MGF Method — Sum of N(3,1) + N(-1,4) + N(5,0.25):\n")
cat("  Theoretical: N(7, 5.25), sd =", round(sqrt(5.25), 4), "\n")
cat("  Simulated mean =", round(mean(Y_sum), 4), "  sd =", round(sd(Y_sum), 4), "\n\n")

# ------ METHOD 4: Jacobian (Beta from Gamma ratio) ------
alpha1 <- 3; alpha2 <- 5; beta_param <- 2
G1 <- rgamma(n, shape = alpha1, scale = beta_param)
G2 <- rgamma(n, shape = alpha2, scale = beta_param)
U_ratio <- G1 / (G1 + G2)
cat("Jacobian — Gamma(3,2)/(Gamma(3,2)+Gamma(5,2)) = Beta(3,5):\n")
cat("  Theoretical mean = alpha1/(alpha1+alpha2) =", round(alpha1/(alpha1+alpha2), 4), "\n")
cat("  Simulated mean   =", round(mean(U_ratio), 4), "\n\n")

# ------ ORDER STATISTICS ------
# 7 draws from Exponential(100), find min
Y_mat <- matrix(rexp(7 * n, rate = 1/100), nrow = 7)
Y_min <- apply(Y_mat, 2, min)
Y_max <- apply(Y_mat, 2, max)
cat("Order Statistics — 7 draws from Exp(100):\n")
cat("  Min: theoretical mean = 100/7 =", round(100/7, 2),
    "  simulated =", round(mean(Y_min), 2), "\n")
cat("  Max: simulated mean =", round(mean(Y_max), 2), "\n\n")

# ------ PROBABILITY INTEGRAL TRANSFORM ------
Y_gamma <- rgamma(n, shape = 4, rate = 1/3)
U_pit <- pgamma(Y_gamma, shape = 4, rate = 1/3)
ks_result <- ks.test(U_pit, "punif")
cat("Probability Integral Transform (Gamma → Uniform):\n")
cat("  KS test p-value =", round(ks_result$p.value, 4),
    "(large p = uniform confirmed)\n\n")

cat("All results match theory. The math works!\n")

These exercises integrate concepts from across the entire chapter.

Let X \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 2). Use the CDF method to find the PDF of U = X^3. Then verify your answer using the transformation method.

Let X \sim N(0, 1). Find the PDF of U = |X| using the CDF method. (This is the “half-normal” distribution — used in Bayesian statistics as a prior for standard deviations.)

Let X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{10} be iid \text{Exponential}(\beta = 5). Find the distribution of U = 2\sum_{i=1}^{10} X_i / \beta. (Hint: first find the distribution of the sum using MGFs, then apply the scaling property of the Gamma family.)

Let X and Y be independent \text{Uniform}(0, 1). Define U = \max(X, Y) and V = \min(X, Y). Find the joint PDF of (U, V) and the PDF of W = U - V (the range).

Let X_1 \sim \text{Gamma}(3, 2) and X_2 \sim \text{Gamma}(5, 2) be independent. Find the distribution of R = X_1 / (X_1 + X_2).

A reliability engineer tests 20 identical light bulbs. Each bulb’s lifetime is iid \text{Exponential}(\beta = 1000) hours.
(a) Find the distribution of the time until the first bulb fails.
(b) What is the expected time until the first failure?
(c) Find P(all 20 bulbs last at least 50 hours).

Let Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_8 be iid N(0,1). Find the distribution of W = Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + \cdots + Z_8^2 and compute P(W > 15.507).

Let Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4, Y_5 be iid from a distribution with CDF F(y) = y^3 for 0 \leq y \leq 1. Find the PDF of the median Y_{(3)}.

A factory makes resistors whose resistance (in ohms) follows a N(100, 4) distribution. Power dissipated is P = V^2/R, where voltage is a constant V = 12 volts. Find the approximate distribution of P using a first-order Taylor expansion: P \approx V^2/\mu_R + (-V^2/\mu_R^2)(R - \mu_R). (This is the “Delta Method” preview.)

(Challenge) Let X and Y be iid \text{Exponential}(1). Use the transformation U = X/(X+Y), V = X + Y to show that U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1) and that U and V are independent. (This is a special case of Example 7.15 with \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = 1, and it explains why \text{Beta}(1, 1) = \text{Uniform}(0,1).)

Dr. Anjana Yatawara

Welcome

This is a free, open-source textbook for a first course in probability theory. It covers the mathematical foundations of probability — from sample spaces and counting to random variables, distributions, and transformations — with every concept illustrated through simulation, every theorem fully proved, and every result verified in R.

Prerequisites: Calculus I and II (integration, series, basic multivariable). No prior statistics course required — Chapter 1 covers the basics you need.

records.content:
Every concept in this book follows a three-step pipeline:

See it. We start with a simulation or a concrete example so you can observe the phenomenon before we formalize it.

Prove it. We prove every result rigorously. No “it can be shown that.” No hand-waving. The proof is where the learning happens.

Simulate it. After the proof, R code confirms the result empirically. You’ll see theory and practice agree — and when they don’t, you’ll understand why.

records.content:
By the end of this book, you will be able to:

Construct probability models for random experiments and compute event probabilities using axioms and counting methods

Derive and apply the major discrete and continuous probability distributions

Work with joint, marginal, and conditional distributions for multiple random variables

Compute expected values, variances, covariances, and moment generating functions

Find the distribution of functions and transformations of random variables

Write R code to simulate, visualize, and verify every result you prove by hand
